articles.title: Natural Cycles wants to create wearable birth control
articles.summary: Natural Cycles is the only app the FDA cleared to be sold as birth control. The company is integrating temperature data from third-party wearables like Oura Ring, and it needs the agency’s sign-off for it to be used in the birth control program.
articles.body: Natural Cycles, the first “digital birth control” to get sign-off from the Food and Drug Administration, is back. This time, it’s asking the agency to authorize integration with wearable devices like the Oura Ring. The feature could make it easier for users to use the app properly, but it doesn’t sidestep some of the existing issues with app-based birth control. The Natural Cycles app uses daily temperature measurements and period cycle tracking to predict the days someone is least likely to get pregnant. It falls under the broad category of fertility awareness birth control methods, where people track when they’d be ovulating and use that information to figure out when they’d have the best chance of conceiving. It tends to be conflated with the rhythm method, which is ineffective, but when done properly, fertility awareness can be as or more effective than hormonal birth control pills. App users have to manually take their temperature each day, right when they wake up in the morning. The new feature would let users pair the app with a wearable device that could take their temperature for them. “We do see that there are some users that have trouble remembering to take their temperature in the morning,” says Elina Berglund, co-founder and CEO of Natural Cycles. “We listened to our users, and they said, you know it would be great if there will be something they could wear and measure the temperature during the night so they don’t have to remember in the morning.” Anyone using the app to track their fertility can use the feature now through a beta program. People who use the app as birth control, which Berglund says is about 75 percent of users, don’t have access yet — Natural Cycles needs sign-off from the FDA first. Right now, the app is only cleared to be used as birth control with a basal body temperature thermometer, which tracks smaller temperature increments than a regular thermometer. The FDA’s initial decision to clear Natural Cycles in 2018 was controversial: the app was blamed for unwanted pregnancies in Sweden and was heavily promoted on social media. Fertility awareness can be an effective method of birth control, but to use the technique, people usually have to learn to track and interpret their daily temperature and other fertility signals, like cervical mucus. Experts say it’s not easy to translate that careful tracking into an app, and it’s not a good option for everyone — like people who have inconsistent menstrual cycles or sleep schedules, for example. Natural Cycles only uses temperature to measure fertility signals, and it doesn’t incorporate other metrics, like cervical mucus. Tracking only one signal tends to be less accurate than tracking both together, research shows. “Temperature is not the king of indicators for fertility awareness,” says Rebecca Simmons, a researcher and fertility awareness specialist at the University of Utah. Using a wearable like an Oura Ring to measure temperature adds another layer of automation to fertility awareness. That has some drawbacks: it removes the app another step further from the body literacy that underlies fertility awareness methods. But it could help app users get a more accurate and consistent read on their temperatures, Simmons says. A wearable would measure temperature continuously, not just at one moment. It may be less thrown by changes in when someone goes to bed or if they’ve had alcohol the night before, she says. Still, it only has those benefits if the ring is taking high-quality temperature measurements. Berglund says that Natural Cycles has completed an internal study on the Oura Ring’s temperature readings, but they haven’t published that data. A small study last year in 22 women found that temperatures measured by the ring and temperatures taken orally were comparable. But research is still limited. “There’s a long way to go before we can feel like, oh yeah, these are really able to tell us what we need to know in order to predict our fertility,” Simmons says. The potential benefits also don’t elevate the app to the level of a more comprehensive fertility awareness approach, she says. “The benefits only outweigh the drawbacks if you’re already using this [app-based] approach, which already divorces you from that fertility literacy.” Partnering with a third-party wearable device may also make it harder for users to understand where their data is going. If it’s just contained in the Natural Cycles app, there’s only one privacy policy and one set of terms and conditions. Adding another device to the equation brings in another set of rules. “It just creates a messier space for people to try to understand their own privacy rights than these apps,” Simmons says. Natural Cycle’s filing to the FDA isn’t specific to Oura Ring — it’s open ended and would let the app integrate with any wearable device that measures temperature. “If we do a small internal study validating a wearable and see that it can give the same quality as the oral thermometer, then it can be used for Natural Cycles,” Berglund says. Berglund says the company will evaluate how the wearable integration is being used and how well it works, both under the beta program and in a full rollout, assuming FDA clearance. Simmons says that’s one thing she appreciates about Natural Cycles. “They really do try to publish their work, they try to utilize the correct channels,” she says. She’s excited about the possibility that people may have better ways to gather information on their fertility, but the research just isn’t quite at the caliber it would need to be for full trust in digital birth control, Simmons says. “We have to have bigger, longer, and better studies that ensure that we feel confident,” she says. “I think that the data are still too sparse to have a lot of confidence that the technology is where it needs to be in order to move forward.”

articles.title: Space collisions could become a bigger risk thanks to greenhouse gas pollution
articles.summary: As space gets more crowded, satellite collisions are a growing problem. Greenhouse gas emissions could raise the risks, research warns.
articles.body: Greenhouse gas emissions could affect satellite launches in the future, new research suggests. As it builds up, the pollution causes Earth’s upper atmosphere to contract, potentially raising the risk of satellite collisions in orbit. It’s yet another way that fossil fuel emissions are having a tangible impact on things people rely on daily, especially as telecommunication companies launch megaconstellations of satellites into orbit. Space, it turns out, is a finite resource — and it’ll have to be better managed as climate change makes things even more restricted, the study authors contend. “We’ve really reached the end of that era of ‘space is big,’ and I think we should stop saying that,” says William Parker, lead author of the study, which was published today in Nature Sustainability, and a PhD candidate at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “People don’t realize that the space sustainability issue is really an issue that impacts them directly.” Greenhouse gas emissions trap heat in the lower atmosphere, raising global average temperatures on Earth. Another side effect is less heat makes it into Earth’s upper atmosphere, and the heat that does dissipates more easily into space. That results in cooling and contraction in the upper atmosphere. You can think of it like a balloon shrinking if you put it in a freezer, Parker says. People rely on a strong atmosphere to eventually pull down dead satellites and other orbiting debris, most of which eventually burns up as it falls through the atmosphere. But as the atmosphere becomes less dense, it reduces drag on space debris, allowing it to linger in orbit for longer — and extending the lifespan it has to crash into other objects. Satellite carrying capacity could decline between 50 to 66 percent between the altitudes of 200 and 1,000 km above Earth, according to the study. That would be 75 years from now, in a worst-case scenario with high greenhouse gas emissions from continued fossil fuel development and increasingly energy-intensive lifestyles on Earth. Fortunately, that means there’s still some time to limit the risks that greenhouse gas emissions could pose to satellites. In a middle-of-the road scenario that’s considered a more likely outcome, with moderate greenhouse gas emissions through the end of the century, carrying capacity at the same altitudes would decrease between 24 to 33 percent. That would still be a significant change that satellite operators would have to prepare for, especially since lower Earth orbit is becoming much more crowded. Humans have launched around 20,650 satellites into space since 1957, around 11,100 of which are still functioning. Those numbers have skyrocketed over the past decade with the advent of satellite internet services. SpaceX’s Starlink alone reportedly has plans to send as many as 42,000 satellites into orbit. Collisions are a growing concern as junk builds up in space. SpaceX satellites had to perform 50,000 collision avoidance maneuvers in just the first half of 2024 to avoid other spacecraft and debris. And as greenhouse gas emissions grow, they may have to maneuver around even more obstacles. There’s been previous research into how greenhouse gas emissions cause shrinking and cooling in the upper atmosphere. The study published today is likely the first attempt to quantify the impact that decreasing atmospheric density has on the orbital capacity of lower Earth orbit, according to Petr Šácha, a researcher in the atmospheric physics department at Charles University who was not involved with the new paper. Parker and his colleagues used atmospheric models to estimate how many satellites can safely orbit in different greenhouse gas emissions scenarios. Šácha notes that there are other factors that could cause short-term anomalies in density, however, particularly considering what little understanding scientists have on how gravity waves will respond to atmospheric changes caused by greenhouse gas emissions. Parker wants to make sure that we can avoid a tipping point where all the traffic in lower Earth orbit triggers cascading collisions, which could lead to humans losing access to certain parts of space, sort of like a road closure after a highway pileup. At this point, humans rely on satellites for everyday services — from GPS to weather forecasts. “We all want to make sure that future generations are able to take advantage of the benefits that we get from space,” Parker says. “I think the goal behind this paper was to engage the public a little bit … space sustainability impacts them. And to make sure that within the satellite operator community, people are aware that this resource is finite and it’s changing.”

articles.title: Starlink’s got company — and orbital overcrowding is a disaster waiting to happen
articles.summary: Amazon’s Project Kuiper satellite mega constellation is just the beginning.
articles.body: On the evening of April 28th, Amazon embarked on its latest venture to rival SpaceX Starlink: the first launch of its Project Kuiper satellites. With 27 satellites now in orbit around the Earth, Amazon joins a growing number of companies working to put more than 1,000 satellites each into space to create their own mega constellation. With all of these objects in orbit, the dangers of overcrowding are increasing, and if any of these objects were to collide, the results could be disastrous. Aside from Amazon and SpaceX, UK-based OneWeb, which merged with French satellite operator Eutelsat in 2023, has its own constellation, and there are several planned by Chinese companies, too. There is the Chinese government-backed Guowang mega constellation, which began its launches last year but remains veiled in secrecy, as well as the commercial Qianfan or Thousand Sails project, which began launches in 2023 and plans to place a total of up to 15,000 satellites in orbit. A recent report from the European Space Agency (ESA) found that over 2,500 objects were launched into low-Earth orbit in 2024, more than five times the number of objects launched in any year prior to 2020. The major chunk of these launches were for commercial satellite constellations, for which the number of launches is increasing annually. The number of active satellites is now comparable to the number of debris pieces in orbit. If current trends in launch continue, ESA estimates there could be almost 50,000 objects larger than 10cm in low-Earth orbit by 2050. Over the next few years, there could be an estimated average of eight satellites launched daily from Earth, or a total mass of four tons of material sent into space daily. These satellites enable communications and internet access in remote locations, and in areas devastated by natural disasters or war. But the space around our planet is getting increasingly congested with both functioning satellites and the junk left behind by older missions — and the problem will worsen as more satellites are launched. Experts agree that we urgently need more comprehensive rules around the management of objects in orbit, but in an increasingly polarized world, the idea of global cooperation to protect space seems more remote than ever. A crowded orbit “There is a race to fill low-Earth orbit,” says debris researcher Vishnu Reddy of the University of Arizona. It’s not only working satellites that are filling up space. There are millions of pieces of junk floating around, many traveling at extremely high speeds. ESA estimates that over 1.2 million objects in orbit are “large enough to be capable of causing catastrophic damage” if they collide with anything. Low-Earth orbit is getting particularly crowded, with thousands of commercial objects in addition to thousands more pieces of debris. The problem isn’t only that debris could damage a vital piece of equipment, such as the International Space Station. If enough collisions of even small debris pieces occur, they could create more and more debris, causing more and more collisions, creating a cascade effect, which could make access to space treacherous, or even require shutting down all global space programs in the future. “The satellite operators are obviously tempted to put more and more satellites,” says astronomer Olivier Hainaut of the European Southern Observatory, who has worked on modeling the brightness of Starlink satellites. “However, if they put too many, there will be collisions. And once you start having collisions, you could have a chain reaction, Kessler syndrome, and you can have a whole range of orbits rendered unusable.” The issue of orbital overcrowding is having effects now. Satellites that are too close together can interfere with each other’s transmissions. Climate change is making the problem worse, too, as the release of greenhouse gases causes the upper atmosphere to shrink, lessening its ability to pull down and destroy debris. No one is suggesting that satellites or even mega constellations should be banned, but launching thousands of objects per year into orbit comes with a downside that isn’t often acknowledged. Researchers are starting to consider where the bounds of orbital capacity might be, and whether the current level of launches is sustainable in the long term. Fending for themselves It isn’t the functioning satellites that are themselves a problem. A satellite owned by a company is going to be tracked and monitored. But there are thousands of pieces of debris already whipping around in low-Earth orbit that are too small to track. The more satellites we put into orbit, the higher the likelihood of collision with a piece of debris. Who is responsible for tracking debris and preventing collisions? No one, essentially. In practice, the space community looks to the US government for tracking information, and hopes that everyone behaves responsibly. “Satellite operators are responsible for their satellites,” Reddy says. “The Space Force tracks a number of objects and updates the catalog a couple of times a day, and the hope is that people will be able to fend for themselves, based on what is freely being provided by the United States.” That extends to disposing of inoperative satellites. SpaceX has been relatively responsible in deorbiting its defunct satellites, experts agreed. As Starlink satellites sit in a very low orbit, after a few years they naturally drop into the Earth’s atmosphere where they break apart. Satellite operators don’t want to be fighting with each other for space, so they each use different orbits. The Project Kuiper satellites, for example, launched into a slightly higher altitude than the Starlink ones. However, it’s still necessary to move satellites through other orbits, which is why orbital crowding is a problem. “What goes up must come down,” Reddy says. “So eventually Kuipers have to deorbit and go through the Starlink orbital range to reenter. What happens then?” After this post was published, Amazon representative Tina Pelkey pointed to posts from the company regarding its plans to safely deorbit satellites and its support of the ESA Zero Debris Charter, but did not respond to specific questions about handling potential conjunctions. ​​Avoiding the bad days Potential conflicts between satellite operators could become a major issue, as avoiding collisions comes with a financial cost. If, say, a Starlink satellite and a Project Kuiper satellite were on a collision course — what experts refer to as a conjunction — then one or both satellites need to adjust their orbit by using up some of their very limited supply of fuel. “Now you have the people at Starlink and Kuiper who have to decide who’s going to burn the gas to avoid hitting each other, and that’s going to eat into their profit,” Reddy says. That’s actually one of the more positive scenarios, because at least Starlink and Project Kuiper satellites have owners who have clear responsibility for them. That isn’t the case for thousands of pieces of smaller debris in orbit. “A good day is when you can have a conjunction between two satellites and both are operating,” Reddy says. “A bad day is when you have two things that don’t work, where the operators have disappeared, and there’s a collision. All you can do is sit and pray they don’t create debris.” It’s virtually impossible to predict exactly how much debris any given collision would create, as it depends on the impact speed and direction, and what the objects are made of. With information about satellite composition sometimes kept proprietary, there’s no way to really know how much damage an impact could do. This situation is compounded by satellite mega constellations, in which thousands of satellites share an orbit. If one satellite malfunctions and explodes, a company may need to move hundreds of its satellites to adjust — and those maneuvers could create even more conjunctions. The situation would be even worse, and even more chaotic, if multiple mega constellations are involved. “The hope is that it won’t happen,” Reddy says. “But when it happens it can go bad really quickly.” Who blinks first Space debris experts like Reddy aren’t against satellite companies making money in space. But he’d like to see these companies take more initiative in creating norms and guidelines around collision prevention: “It’s in their own financial interest to come up with the ground set of rules.” The companies don’t need to wait for the slow process of international agreement to take an active role in managing this issue. “SpaceX has a lot more experience running a mega constellation than any regulator we can find on Earth,” he says, and they could make proposals on handling conjunction events — “So the burden is not on the world governments to come up with a plan.” It’s also, frankly, better for the satellite companies themselves to take this issue seriously and avoid the significant risk that collisions can pose, especially as more and more companies are launching mega constellations of their own — including companies from outside the US. What happens when, say, there are hundreds of potential conjunction events between Starlink satellites and Chinese mega constellation satellites, he wondered. With stakes this high, the question becomes: “Who’s gonna move? Are we going to sit there and see who blinks first?” There needs to be a formal system of cooperation between satellite companies, agreeing on how to make maneuvers in the case of two satellites heading for each other, Reddy says. “It’s a much better thing than to say, okay, we’re gonna have a collision in three hours. Let’s try and scramble through the phone book and find out who in China I need to call. That’s not a good way to do business.” A near miss The threat of a collision between satellites is not purely theoretical. In 2019, disaster almost struck when there was a near miss between a Starlink satellite and a European Space Agency (ESA) Aeolus satellite. ESA had to make a last-minute correction maneuver of its satellite to avoid a collision, which could have thrown debris across a large area of the orbit had it occurred. That would be concerning in any event, but this case was particularly worrying because ESA tried and failed to contact SpaceX to raise the issue and coordinate the movement of the satellites. SpaceX said at the time that ESA’s email warning of the collision had been overlooked due to a “bug.” The problem then, as now, is that there is no legal framework for dealing with these kinds of potential satellite collisions. We need rules similar to those for air traffic control but for space, experts agree, but those rules don’t currently exist — and a conjunction could happen at any time. The near miss between Aeolus and Starlink 44 was “a template for what we see every day,” said Holger Krag, ESA’s Head of Space Safety Programme, at a space debris conference earlier this month. “Whenever two active spacecraft encounter each other you have to rely on cooperation. You will have to communicate, you have to coordinate action,” Krag said. However, there are currently no laws or rules making it clear whose responsibility this communication is, or how collisions should be avoided. “We are far away from a clear flight rule that would solve exactly the situation that Aeolus and Starlink had,” Krag said. Further, as the number of satellites in orbit increases, ESA has warned that the current process for manually averting collisions by individually adjusting the position of each satellite will become impossible. To create a system of enforceable laws regarding the use of orbital space would require an international resolution by a body like the United Nations, because no one nation can regulate space. But there is little international will to make that happen. The last significant piece of international space legislation, on which current law is still based, was the Outer Space Treaty passed nearly 60 years ago in 1967. That treaty never imagined operations in space by private companies, though, leaving a regulatory vacuum over whose responsibility issues like space debris are. This is a classic tragedy of the commons. No one wants space to become inaccessible, but few groups are willing or able to tackle the issue directly. Josef Aschbacher, the director general of ESA, summed up the problem at the conference: “The message is crystal clear: space debris is a problem and we have to do something about it.” Update April 29th, 2025: Added a note from Amazon.

articles.title: Satellites keep photobombing the Hubble telescope, and it’s getting worse
articles.summary: Astronomers are going to increasingly struggle to take images in space without satellites interfering, researchers warn.
articles.body: It’s getting harder and harder for the Hubble and other telescopes orbiting Earth to capture pristine images thanks to the sudden surge in satellite launches. Satellite trails could mess up nearly 40 percent of images the Hubble takes and up to 96 percent of those taken by three other telescopes over the next decade, according to a study by NASA researchers published today in the journal Nature. That could jeopardize scientists’ ability to spot worrisome asteroids or discover new planets, they warn. Our view of space just gets fuzzier without efforts to limit light pollution from new megaconstellations of satellites. “My career has been focused on trying to make telescopes see better … try to make the telescopes more sensitive, more precise, getting better images,” says Alejandro Borlaff, a NASA research scientist and lead author of the study. “For the first time, we found something that may actually be worse in the future.” The scale of the problem is astounding. Cheaper launch costs and the proliferation of telecommunications satellites like Starlink’s have opened up a Pandora’s box of new challenges in space. Satellite trails, which look like streaks of light, were already detected in 4.3 percent of images taken by the Hubble between 2018 and 2021. The number of satellites orbiting Earth has grown from 5,000 in 2019 to more than 15,800 today, according to the European Space Agency. That number could reach as high as 560,000 if currently planned satellite launches proceed over the next 10 years or so. Borlaff and his colleagues simulated the view that four telescopes are likely to have after all those launches. With that much crowding in space, they project that the Hubble telescope could inadvertently capture an average of 2.14 satellites per exposure. The Chinese Space Station Telescope Xuntian, one of the other telescopes included in the study that’s expected to launch next year, could see an average of 92 satellites per exposure. The Hubble is less likely to catch as many satellites in its images because of its narrower field of view. Fortunately, other powerful telescopes, including the James Webb, orbit far enough from Earth to avoid light contamination from satellites. [Media: The issue goes beyond accidentally including a satellite (or many) among the visions of swirling nebulae, stars, and distant planets these telescopes capture. The satellites reflect light from the Sun, Moon, or Earth, which can be bright enough to obscure details that might otherwise be captured in an image were it not for that light pollution. Researchers might not be able to detect a change in the brightness of a star that could indicate that there’s an exoplanet there, Borlaff explains. “You will lose that information because a satellite passed in front of you.” Now’s the time to find solutions, he says, before there are so many satellites in orbit. Efforts to design darker, less reflective satellites have posed new problems because they tend to get hotter and shed more infrared light as a result. Researchers have also tried strategizing to take images at times and locations with a lower likelihood of satellites crossing their path, an endeavor that’s harder to do the more crowded it gets out there. It’ll take more coordination on the ground with companies and governments launching satellites, maybe by placing them in orbit lower than where the telescopes are to avoid obstructing their view or regulating where they can be deployed. “There has to be an optimal way to place constellations and space telescopes … so we can coexist in a sustainable way,” Borlaff says.

articles.title: Natural Cycles launches wristband to replace thermometers for its FDA-cleared birth control app
articles.summary: The FDA-cleared digital birth control app Natural Cycles is launching a new wristband designed to track your temperature, heart rate, and movement while you sleep, allowing the accompanying app to determine your fertility status.
articles.body: Natural Cycles, the company behind a controversial FDA-cleared birth control app, is replacing its thermometer with a wristband that measures skin temperature, heart rate, and movement during sleep. The newly launched wristband costs $129.99 and syncs with the Natural Cycles app, which uses an algorithm to determine a person’s “daily fertility status.” Users can already track their fertility by pairing an Apple Watch or Oura Ring with Natural Cycles, but the wristband could be an option for users who don’t have either of these devices handy. While Natural Cycles also works with newer Samsung Galaxy smartwatches and the Galaxy Ring, it’s meant for temperature-based period and cycle tracking when used with these devices — not as a way to prevent or plan pregnancy. The FDA cleared Natural Cycles as a form of birth control in 2018, a decision that proved controversial, as it came after 37 of 668 women seeking an abortion at a Swedish hospital reported unwanted pregnancies while using the app. (Swedish regulators said the app was not malfunctioning and that it maintained the same failure rate as advertised by Natural Cycles.) Some critics argued that the device received less scrutiny from the FDA when compared to other forms of contraception. Natural Cycles initially offered a basal thermometer with its annual plan (or available separately for $14.50) so users could take their temperatures manually. Natural Cycles spokesperson Lauren Hanafin tells The Verge that users can continue using the thermometer if they currently have one. The FDA later gave Natural Cycles approval to collect data from third-party devices, like the Apple Watch and the Oura Ring. Hanafin says the company received authorization from the FDA to start using other temperature-tracking wearables without requiring additional approval, allowing it to launch the new wristband. [Image: [Image: Privacy concerns related to period-tracking apps grew following the Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade, but the Electronic Frontier Foundation notes that while users should review the security and privacy protections of the app they choose, they aren’t an “immediate threat” to abortion-seekers. Natural Cycles says it uses pseudonymization and encryption to conceal your information, while its band only collects data that’s “necessary.” Natural Cycles first introduced its wristband to “select” people as part of the launch of its perimenopause feature in October. The band supports Bluetooth 5.0 LE and offers a battery life of up to 14 nights after it’s fully charged via USB-C. The Natural Cycles Band is available for purchase for $129.99, and is also included with the company’s annual plan for $149.99. Users who already have a Natural Cycles subscription can upgrade to the band for $99.99 for a limited time. Update, January 16th: Added Swedish regulator response.

articles.title: FOTOS e VÍDEOS: a captura da Starship, da SpaceX, por braços mecânicos | G1
articles.standfirst: Nave foi disparada para a órbita da Terra no sábado (13) e, no retorno, foi capturada no ar por braços mecânicos na mesma plataforma de lançamento. Técnica pretende diminuir os custos do uso de foguetes.
articles.summary: Nave foi disparada para a órbita da terra no sábado (13) e, no retorno, foi capturada no ar por braços mecânicos na mesma plataforma de lançamento de onde havia partido.
articles.body:
A SpaceX divulgou nesta segunda-feira (16) imagens do retorno à Terra da Starship. As imagens mostram o momento de pouso da nave espacial em voo realizado no sábado (14). Veja as fotos no fim da reportagem .

A nave foi disparada para a órbita da Terra e, no retorno, foi capturada no ar por braços mecânicos na mesma plataforma de lançamento de onde havia partido. O objetivo da missão era justamente a primeira captura de uma Starship que retornava do espaço.

Starship, nave da SpaceX, retorna à base depois de alcançar a órbita da Terra — Foto: Divulgação

Representantes da SpaceX afirmaram que a captura feita no sábado demonstra a capacidade de reutilização completa da Starship, projetada para viagens à Lua e a Marte.

Um dia antes, na sexta-feira (13), uma outra missão da SpaceX terminou com a explosão do propulsor de primeiro estágio pouco depois da decolagem no Texas. Destroços permaneceram no Golfo do México, isolados por boias, enquanto a espaçonave de aço inoxidável, em formato de projétil, descia na vertical até a plataforma de lançamento.

Embora a tentativa de recuperação do propulsor na sexta-feira tenha fracassado, a empresa já havia realizado outras três capturas bem-sucedidas, validando a técnica.

A Nasa comemorou a notícia deste sábado. A agência espacial está pagando bilhões de dólares pelo desenvolvimento da Starship para transportar astronautas da missão Artemis até a superfície da Lua ainda nesta década.

Com o avanço do projeto, o objetivo da Nasa é ajudar na construção de uma base lunar permanente. Já as ambições de Musk são ainda maiores: ele quer lançar uma frota de Starships para construir uma cidade em Marte.

articles.title: Can ‘sunscreen’ for lakes, dams shield water from evaporation?
articles.summary: A physicist from Ghana has an unusual solution for a serious problem: apply a ‘sunscreen’ to the surface of lakes and reservoirs to conserve water.
articles.body: A physicist from Ghana has an unusual solution for a serious problem: apply a ‘sunscreen’ to the surface of lakes and reservoirs to conserve water.Daniel Kwasi Kpeglo (PhD from University of South Africa), and his team investigated whether a thin, nanomaterial-coated sheet could reduce evaporation while allowing enough light through to sustain aquatic life.They used a commercially available transparent conducting oxide (TCO) and applied it to a standard PET sheet. The researchers published their findings in ‘Nature’.“The most important resource we use is water and much of that is lost to evaporation,” Kpeglo tells TOI. “So we said, ‘Let’s come up with a thin material that will act as a barrier and minimise evaporation’.”Kpeglo says the research began in 2022-23. In the lab, researchers used a 29.8x21.1x11 cm reservoir and a halogen lamp set to 1.5 times the intensity of sunlight, testing at distances of 10, 20 and 30cm. They compared an uncovered reservoir with PET-covered and TCO-coated versions, measuring temperature changes and water loss.In the uncovered reservoir, water levels fell at rates ranging from 0.45mm to 0.78mm per hour, depending on the lamp’s distance. Ordinary PET slowed the loss but did not prevent it. With the coated sheet, the level remained virtually constant during the observation period, within the margin of experimental error. Evaporation was also considerably higher under infrared-rich illumination.The hydrophobic coating could limit biological build-up, although its ability to resist algae and bacteria over time remains untested. Kpeglo says the thin film is not placed directly on the surface of the water. “The sheet is secured above the water, leaving a gap of about one centimetre.”That flexibility could prove useful in India, where monsoon rainfall makes permanent reservoir coverings impractical. “When the rainfall is coming, you can remove it from the reservoir,” Kpeglo says. “You bring it back during the dry season,” he says.The material is far from field ready, however. Wind and moving water could displace the sheets, requiring secure support (see box), and the film’s UV resistance needs to be studied, Kpeglo says. The next step is field trials.The ‘sunscreen’ solution remains a concept, for now, but Kpeglo says it's one with potential. “This thing has opened a door when it comes to using nanosciences to minimise water evaporation.”Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Aneel tem 4 votos a favor de recomendar fim da concessão da Enel em SP, mas diretor-geral pede vista | G1
articles.standfirst: Quatro dos cinco diretores votaram a favor da recomendação de caducidade; Sandoval Feitosa Neto pediu mais tempo para analisar o processo, e votação será retomada. Mesmo após eventual aprovação, decisão final caberá ao Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME).
articles.summary: Quatro dos cinco diretores votaram a favor da recomendação de caducidade; Sandoval Feitosa Neto pediu mais tempo para analisar o processo, e votação será retomada. Mesmo após eventual aprovação, decisão final caberá ao Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME).
articles.body:
Diretos da Aneel durante reunião pública nesta terça (17). — Foto: Reprodução

A diretoria da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) teve quatro votos favoráveis à recomendação de encerramento antecipado da concessão da Enel Distribuição São Paulo, responsável pelo fornecimento de energia elétrica na capital paulista e em municípios da Região Metropolitana, nesta terça-feira (17).

Apesar da maioria favorável, a agência ainda não concluiu a votação. O diretor-geral da Aneel, Sandoval de Araújo Feitosa Neto, pediu vista do processo, ou seja, mais tempo para analisar o caso. Com isso, o julgamento foi suspenso e o placar ainda pode mudar quando a votação for retomada.

A diretoria colegiada da Aneel é composta por cinco integrantes. Votaram a favor da recomendação os diretores Gentil Nogueira de Sá Júnior, Willamy Moreira Frota, Agnes Maria de Aragão da Costa e Ludimila Lima da Silva. Sandoval foi o único integrante da diretoria que não apresentou voto nesta etapa do julgamento.

O processo foi instaurado em abril deste ano, após a agência apontar uma série de falhas na prestação do serviço pela concessionária , identificadas em fiscalizações (leia mais abaixo).

Ainda não há data para a votação ser retomada. Até a conclusão do julgamento, não há decisão definitiva da Aneel sobre a recomendação, e a operação da Enel e o contrato de concessão permanecem inalterados.

Mesmo que a recomendação seja aprovada ao fim da votação, ela ainda precisará ser encaminhada ao Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), a quem caberá decidir sobre a eventual extinção da concessão.

O processo foi instaurado em abril deste ano, após a agência apontar uma série de falhas na prestação do serviço pela concessionária, identificadas em fiscalizações. Entre os problemas analisados estão as dificuldades da empresa para responder a situações de emergência e restabelecer o fornecimento de energia após apagões.

Em seu voto, acompanhado pela diretora Ludimila Lima da Silva, a relatora recomendou ao Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) a caducidade da concessão — medida que representa a extinção antecipada do contrato.

"A recomendação de caducidade decorre da constatação de que todos os instrumentos regulatórios disponíveis à Aneel foram esgotados na tentativa de fazer com que a concessionária corrigisse as falhas ao atendimento em situações de emergência", escreveu Agnes.

🔎 Considerada uma medida extrema, a caducidade (ou extinção do contrato) pode ocorrer quando confirmado que a concessionária descumpre obrigações contratuais e não tem condições de manter a prestação de serviços à população.

O contrato atual da Enel se encerra em 2028, mas a Prefeitura de São Paulo cobra uma reformulação nos critérios de avaliação da empresa antes que qualquer renovação seja considerada.

A Enel detém uma concessão federal gerida pela Aneel para distribuir energia elétrica em 24 municípios da região metropolitana, incluindo a capital, atualmente atendendo cerca de 8 milhões de pessoas (leia mais abaixo).

Ao longo do processo, a Enel vem contestando as conclusões da fiscalização. A concessionária sustenta que sua resposta aos eventos climáticos vem melhorando e afirma que os indicadores de atendimento emergencial evoluíram nos últimos anos.

Subestação da Enel no Cambuci, em São Paulo — Foto: Amanda Perobelli/Reuters

A situação da concessão da Enel SP vem sendo acompanhada pela Aneel desde 2023, período marcado por grandes interrupções no fornecimento de energia na Região Metropolitana de São Paulo .

Entre os episódios que levaram ao aumento da fiscalização estão os apagões registrados após eventos climáticos extremos em novembro de 2023, outubro de 2024 e dezembro de 2025 .

Em outubro de 2024, um temporal atingiu a Grande São Paulo com rajadas de vento de até 107,6 km/h. A Enel informou que 3,1 milhões de clientes chegaram a ser afetados. Seis dias depois da tempestade, a concessionária anunciou que havia normalizado o atendimento das ocorrências relacionadas ao temporal.

Em dezembro de 2025, um novo episódio provocou interrupções em larga escala. Rajadas chegaram a a 98,1 km/h e milhões de imóveis foram afetados.

A fiscalização realizada depois desse episódio identificou problemas na gestão da crise, na mobilização das equipes, na disponibilidade de veículos e equipamentos , no planejamento de contingência e na manutenção preventiva da rede.

Entre as falhas apontadas estavam a concentração de equipes no horário comercial , redução do efetivo durante a noite e a madrugada, uso insuficiente de veículos de grande porte, baixa resolutividade dos atendimentos e deficiências no controle da vegetação próxima à rede elétrica.

Dados analisados pela Aneel mostraram que, das 6.715 ocorrências de interrupção registradas em 10 de dezembro, 3.056 — o equivalente a 46% — demoraram mais de 24 horas para serem solucionadas. Essas ocorrências atingiram 759.304 unidades consumidoras.

Houve casos em que o fornecimento só foi restabelecido quase seis dias depois. A interrupção mais longa registrada durou 142,8 horas.

Em agosto, ao analisar um recurso apresentado pela Enel, o diretor-geral da Aneel, Sandoval Feitosa, afirmou que a fiscalização da concessão vinha identificando problemas desde 2023.

“Desde 2023, temos um conjunto de eventos envolvendo essa concessão. As áreas de fiscalização, que têm sua missão de acompanhar a prestação de serviço, ao longo de todos esses anos firmou um plano de resultados com a companhia — na sua grande maioria desrespeitados, não cumpridos, multas aplicadas, muitas delas não pagas pela empresa”, afirmou na ocasião.

A Procuradoria Federal junto à Aneel também defendeu o prosseguimento do processo.

Segundo parecer da Procuradoria, a análise não se restringe ao desempenho da empresa durante um único evento climático, mas considera um conjunto de falhas apontadas pela fiscalização.

Entre os problemas citados estão o elevado tempo médio de atendimento a ocorrências emergenciais, interrupções superiores a 24 horas, deficiências no planejamento para eventos climáticos extremos e baixa produtividade das equipes responsáveis pela recomposição da rede.

A empresa alegava que o processo envolvia questões de alta complexidade técnica, incluindo aspectos meteorológicos, operacionais, estatísticos e regulatórios.

A Aneel entendeu, porém, que os elementos técnicos reunidos durante a fiscalização eram suficientes para a análise e encerrou a fase de instrução do processo, abrindo prazo para as alegações finais da concessionária.

A agência destacou ainda que a severidade dos eventos climáticos não estava em discussão. O ponto central do processo era avaliar se a distribuidora tinha estrutura operacional, planejamento e capacidade de resposta compatíveis com suas obrigações para garantir a prestação adequada do serviço.

Em setembro, a Justiça de São Paulo reconheceu falhas da Enel na prestação do serviço durante o apagão provocado pelo evento climático de dezembro de 2025.

A decisão apontou problemas na gestão da crise, na mobilização das equipes e na manutenção da rede elétrica.

A Justiça rejeitou o argumento de que a intensidade do fenômeno climático seria suficiente para afastar a responsabilidade da concessionária. Segundo a decisão, tempestades, vendavais e ciclones fazem parte dos riscos previsíveis da atividade de distribuição de energia e a empresa deve manter infraestrutura e capacidade operacional para reduzir seus impactos.

Ao longo do processo, a Enel vem contestando as conclusões da fiscalização.

A concessionária sustenta que sua resposta aos eventos climáticos vem melhorando e afirma que os indicadores de atendimento emergencial evoluíram nos últimos anos.

Sobre o evento de dezembro de 2025, a empresa afirmou que a atuação foi compatível com a magnitude do fenômeno e que os ventos fortes e prolongados foram o principal fator responsável pelos danos.

A Enel também afirmou que conseguiu restabelecer o fornecimento para 2,5 milhões de unidades consumidoras em nove horas e que, em 24 horas, 80% dos clientes afetados já estavam com o serviço normalizado.

A empresa sustenta ainda que dados da própria Aneel demonstram que seu desempenho em emergências é compatível com o de outras grandes distribuidoras submetidas a eventos climáticos de magnitude semelhante.

articles.title: Madagascar has taken a step towards funding the protection of 4 million hectares of forests across 13 regions, nearly 55% of its forest cover, under a carbon-credit programme targeting 6 million tonnes of annual emissions reductions.
articles.summary: For millennia, forests have been our primary source of natural resources.
articles.body: For millennia, forests have been our primary source of natural resources. Not only have they provided us with food, wood and shelter, but they have also helped develop civilisation. From Christmas trees to the sacred groves of tribal communities, forests have shaped traditions beyond cultural boundaries. But today, as deforestation and climate change threaten these ecosystems, it might be time we did something in return. We have destroyed forests for money through illegal poaching, deforestation and the pursuit of short-term economic gains. But what if I told you that a small island nation in Africa has found a way to monetise forest protection?According to a November 12 announcement by the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS), Madagascar's initiative, known as Ala Velona, meaning 'Living Forests', aims to protect approximately 4 million hectares of forests across 13 regions, representing nearly 55% of the country's forest cover.The announcement follows the publication of the programme's formal concept note on the registry of the Architecture for REDD+ Transactions (ART), an international organisation that administers the TREES standard for forest carbon credits.“Madagascar deserves recognition for taking this important step toward long-term, equitable security for its extraordinary forests and biodiversity,” said Joe Walston, WCS Executive Vice President for Global Conservation. “By pursuing high-integrity forest carbon credits, the government demonstrates how protecting nature can directly support communities, build resilience and contribute to countering climate change. We look forward to continuing our partnership with the government and people of Madagascar on this ambitious initiative.”How does Madagascar's carbon-credit programme work?Imagine a forest that does not have to be cut down to generate economic value. Its trees remain standing, its wildlife continues to thrive, and the communities living around it can benefit from its protection. This is the idea behind Madagascar's Ala Velona, which translates to 'Living Forests'.The programme is built around the concept of carbon credits. In simple terms, when a country demonstrates that it has reduced greenhouse gas emissions by preventing deforestation and forest degradation, it can earn carbon credits for those verified reductions. These credits can then be sold to generate funding for further conservation efforts.Madagascar's programme aims to protect approximately 4 million hectares of forests across 13 regions, with a target of reducing emissions by 6 million tonnes annually. However, the programme must still go through the required registration, validation and verification processes before carbon credits can be issued.But why is there suddenly so much emphasis on protecting forests?Why are Madagascar's forests worth protecting?Madagascar is not just another island with dense forests. It is considered one of the world's most important biodiversity hotspots, with an extraordinary variety of plants and animals, many of which cannot be found anywhere else in the world. According to the Convention on Biological Diversity, approximately 96% of its vascular plant species, 90% of its reptiles and all its lemur species are endemic to the island. This makes Madagascar's forests particularly important, as they serve as natural habitats for species that have evolved in relative isolation for millions of years.Among its most recognisable inhabitants are lemurs, the primates native to Madagascar, alongside colourful chameleons, rare orchids and baobab trees. Its forests also provide essential ecological services, helping regulate water systems, protect soil and support the livelihoods of communities dependent on agriculture and other natural resources. According to the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), rural communities in Madagascar depend heavily on these natural resources for their livelihoods and food security.However, for a long time now, this ecological wealth has been under pressure. Agricultural expansion, charcoal production, illegal logging, mining and forest fires continue to contribute to habitat destruction and degradation. A 2026–2030 strategic plan by WWF Madagascar identifies habitat destruction as the leading threat to the island's endemic species, around 90% of which are dependent on forests.The consequences extend beyond wildlife. As forests disappear, communities also risk losing their resources and the culture that comes with them, their livelihoods and, ultimately, their very future. With continued soil degradation and disruption of water systems, the threat is not only to the trees but also to the children of these communities. Protecting Madagascar's forests, therefore, is not simply about preserving rare species; it is also about safeguarding the natural systems and human communities that depend on themYour child uses AI every day. articles.title: Scientists Just Found Something Strange Under the Skin of Sea Pigs
articles.summary: The translucent blobs of flesh that are sea pigs are some of the most unusual sights in the deep ocean. They're also difficult to study. Some of them live mo...
articles.body:
The translucent blobs of flesh that are sea pigs are some of the most unusual sights in the deep ocean. They're also difficult to study. Some of them live more than 32,800 feet below the surface, so getting eyes on them isn't easy.

Now researchers have made a new discovery about the microbes that call these sea pigs home. Having symbiotic bacteria living under the skin isn't unusual for these types of creatures, but a recent study published in ISME Host Microbe details what could be a new species and a new genus of such bacteria.

The microbes were found in eight sea pigs collected off the northern coast of Japan in the Northwest Pacific, and they dominated the body walls of the echinoderms—76.4 to 98.9 percent of the bacterial DNA found under the skin was this new species.

"Taxonomic and genomic information about these body-wall inhabiting bacteria is scarce, and very few studies of deep-sea species have linked this information to the bacteria's location within host tissues," study author Yu Yoshida explained in a statement .

Not only is the bacteria new, it's rather strange as well. It has a stripped-down genome (set of DNA instructions), and yet, it's still capable of producing giant proteins to carry out work inside cells. The biggest protein the researchers found was 5,475 amino acids long, compared to around 300 for an average bacterial protein.

The study team has suggested Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola for the name of the new species, which roughly translates as the "abyss-dweller that lives in Scotoplanes " ( Scotoplanes being the genus of the sea pig).

So what does this mean for the jelly-like sea pigs, which waddle along at the bottom of the ocean, picking up dead bits of matter with their tubular feet? Well, we're not sure. The assumption is they have some kind of mutually beneficial relationship that's not yet obvious to us.

This much we do know, though: For the inhabitants of the deep ocean, sea pigs are a vital part of the ecosystem. They recycle nutrients and protect other marine life against predators, which is why scientists are keen to learn more about how they thrive and how they've evolved.

"We'd really like to understand how this bacterium could become so dominant in the body wall, the functions of the giant surface proteins, what competition it faces from other bacteria, and the effects on the host," added Yoshida.

Of course, another literal deep dive will be needed to find out more.

articles.title: Nearly 3,000 square kilometres of mangroves were lost between 1984 and 2010; satellite images now reveal a global recovery, with almost 2,000 sq km of mangrove forests growing back
articles.summary: For decades, mangrove forests were considered one of the world’s most threatened coastal ecosystems.
articles.body: For decades, mangrove forests were considered one of the world’s most threatened coastal ecosystems. A new study from Tulane University has found signs of mangrove forests recovering worldwide. Mangroves had been disappearing for decades, but new growth has helped reverse much of that damage. The study is based on four decades of satellite data. The findings are published in the journal Science.Mangroves are bouncing backThe new study by researchers at Tulane University has found that coastal forests are no longer in net decline worldwide. Mangroves are finally bouncing back in many regions after decades of losses accelerated by deforestation and coastal development. So how did this recovery happen? The answer is less complicated than it might seem. Natural regeneration and expansion into newly formed coastal areas are helping drive the process. These findings offer new hope, as mangroves play a crucial role in protecting coastlines, supporting fisheries and helping slow climate change.“After decades of loss, we’re finally seeing a global turning point for mangroves. This highlights their strong resilience and their potential as a powerful nature-based solution for climate mitigation and coastal protection,” Zhen Zhang, a postdoctoral scholar at Tulane University School of Science and Engineering and lead author of the study, said in a release.Loss and rebirthMangroves lost nearly 2,900 square kilometres between 1984 and 2010. Since then, gains have outpaced losses. The researchers recorded an increase of almost 2,000 square kilometres after 2010. By 2023, the net decline over the full four decades had shrunk to about 1 per cent, a much smaller loss than earlier estimates had suggested.“What we’re seeing now is a real shift. Mangroves are now showing a net increase globally, and the rate of degradation is slowing,” Daniel Friess, Cochran Family Professor of Earth and Environmental Sciences at Tulane and director of The Mangrove Lab, said.“While some mangroves are still being lost, this could make them a rare conservation success story and an important source of optimism for climate action,” said Friess, who also serves as director of the Center for Public Policy Research at the Murphy Institute.What’s driving the change? Restoration work and natural regeneration are both contributing. In many regions, mangroves are reclaiming abandoned aquaculture ponds and spreading onto new mudflats, particularly in river deltas where sediment creates good growing conditions.The trend is also visible along the U.S. Gulf Coast. However, the process driving it is different. In the Mississippi River Delta, mangrove area dipped slightly from the 1980s through the late 1990s, then began to climb, with faster growth after 2012. Researchers link most of that growth to warmer temperatures, which allow mangroves to spread into higher-latitude areas that were once too cold for them. Louisiana has also seen an overall increase over the past four decades.The researchers also noticed something encouraging beyond the growth. Many existing mangrove forests are becoming denser and healthier. Closed-canopy forests, which store more carbon and offer better protection to coastlines, have expanded globally over the past four decades. Rates of degradation have dropped significantly since the 1980s, which the researchers attribute to conservation policies and restoration programmes.The researchers noted that consistent protection is essential to sustain this regrowth. “The most immediate and effective way to protect mangroves is to stop deforestation. When mangroves are cleared, large amounts of long-stored carbon are released into the atmosphere. But when deforestation stops, mangroves can continue to accumulate carbon naturally over time, so there’s a major climate benefit in both avoiding emissions now and allowing future carbon storage,” Zhang said. He also added that protecting the natural processes that support mangrove growth is equally important.“Much of mangrove expansion happens on newly formed mudflats, which depend on a steady supply of river sediment. Maintaining that sediment flow is critical for creating the conditions mangroves need to establish and spread,” Zhang explained. He also argued that conservation efforts should look beyond total area. “As countries invest in nature-based solutions to climate change, mangroves stand out as a rare example of an ecosystem where global trends are beginning to move in the right direction,” Zhang said.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Uber and Zipline’s drone delivery service takes flight in Houston
articles.summary: Uber Eats is launching drone delivery in partnership with Zipline in Spring, Texas, with plans to expand to Dallas and hit 1 million daily flights by 2029.
articles.body: Uber Eats is officially launching drone delivery in partnership with Zipline starting Tuesday. The initial rollout begins in the Houston suburb of Spring, Texas, with Dallas next in line and dozens of additional US cities planned. The rollout comes after Uber and Zipline first announced their tie-up, including an investment in Zipline by Uber, back in August 2026. The companies have set the ambitious goal to hit 1 million drone deliveries per day by the end of 2029. Spring residents in the coverage area will see a new “Drone” icon in the Uber app’s home screen to browse participating restaurants. At checkout, customers will need to confirm a clear drop-off zone in the yard, and can track the drone in real-time via the app. Because the system is fully autonomous, tipping is disabled — though customers can still rate the experience in the app. Unlike other low-hovering delivery drones, Zipline’s aircraft cruise at over 300 feet at speeds up to 70 mph. The drone hovers high overhead and lowers a tethered delivery pod onto the customer’s doorstep or yard. The drones dynamically calculate flight paths based on wind, altitude, and speed — dipping their noses to accelerate or pitching upward to brake as quietly as possible. The drones are built to fly in rain and poor weather, carrying up to 8 pounds of cargo within a 10-mile radius of the restaurant. The initial plan is to operate daily from 8AM to 10PM, Uber says. Customers can order from national chains like Jersey Mike’s and Zaxby’s, alongside dozens of Houston-area staples such as Urban Bird and Abu Omar Halal. To be sure, the “1 million deliveries a day by 2029” target is very aggressive, especially considering that Zipline currently averages roughly one delivery every 20 seconds globally, or around 4,300 a day. Still, delivery drones are becoming a more widely adopted technology in many communities across the US, with Uber competing alongside other players like Amazon Prime Air and Google-backed Wing.

articles.title: NASA investigates mysterious 'potato chip' shapes on Mars as scientists hunt for answers
articles.summary: NASA says its Curiosity rover is probing chip-shaped crystal formations in Martian bedrock at the Nazca site, using SAM and ChemCam to analyze their makeup.
articles.body: NASA scientists are investigating unusual "potato chip-shaped" formations on Mars as they seek to determine how these shapes formed — and just what they're made of, exactly. The news was announced in NASA's "Curiosity" blog on Nov. 11. Curiosity is a NASA rover that has been exploring Mars since 2012. It examined the unusual formations during a drilling campaign at a site nicknamed "Nazca" last week. TREASURE HUNTER STRIKES GOLD WITH 1,000-YEAR-OLD DISCOVERY LINKED TO 'HAND OF GOD' The Nazca drill site is located in a Martian area where scientists have observed unusual disk-shaped features in the bedrock. "This is an area characterized by bedrock containing disk-shaped (or, in a liberal interpretation, potato-chip shaped) crystal forms," the NASA blog said. Images of the Martian bedrock show irregular, curled formations embedded in the rock, some with shapes resembling potato chips. PUZZLING SOUND IN BACKYARD LEADS HOMEOWNER TO MASSIVE 1,000-YEAR-OLD TREASURE NASA said one of its key objectives is to "better characterize these chip-shaped features." Samples collected from the Nazca drill hole were delivered to Curiosity's Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument, an onboard laboratory designed to analyze the chemical makeup of Martian samples. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Curiosity also planned to use its laser-equipped ChemCam instrument to examine a crystal-shaped formation nicknamed "Colca" to gather information about its chemical composition. Scientists also planned to use the Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), a camera mounted on Curiosity's robotic arm, to photograph the crystal-shaped formations at night using white-light and ultraviolet LED lamps. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "ChemCam LIBS observations were planned for each sol including a cluster of crystal forms, a resistant layer in the side of the Nazca block and a dark float rock," NASA's blog stated. The rover was then expected to leave the Nazca drill site and return to its southward route to continue exploring Mars as part of its Friday plan. Fox News Digital reached out to NASA to ask more about the chip-shaped formations and whether they've been observed before. articles.title: An endangered rattlesnake gives birth to 9 babies at a Chicago zoo after nearly 10 years; newborns carry the genetic legacy of one of the region's last populations
articles.summary: An endangered eastern massasauga rattlesnake has given birth to 9 young ones at Lincoln Park Zoo in Chicago, marking the first birth of the species at the
articles.body: An endangered eastern massasauga rattlesnake has given birth to 9 young ones at Lincoln Park Zoo in Chicago, marking the first birth of the species at the zoo in almost a decade. The arrival is an important development for conservation efforts involving one of the region’s rarest snake populations. More than just a new generation of animals, the newborns carry the genetic legacy of what may be the last remaining eastern massasauga rattlesnakes in Cook County, Illinois, giving researchers another reason to continue protecting the species.Nine endangered eastern massasauga rattlesnakes born at Chicago zooThe 9 newborn snakes arrived on January 14, 2026, at Lincoln Park Zoo’s Regenstein Small Mammal-Reptile House. According to the zoo’s January 29 announcement, the birth was particularly significant because eastern massasauga rattlesnakes are considered difficult to breed, and this was the first time the species had produced offspring at the institution in nearly 10 years.The mother is an 11-year-old female born at Lincoln Park Zoo, while the father is a 10-year-old male who has lived at the institution since 2021. Their offspring are part of a carefully planned breeding effort recommended by the Eastern Massasauga Rattlesnake SAFE programme, an initiative of the Association of Zoos and Aquariums that works to protect threatened animal populations.The birth also represents an important step in preserving a local genetic line. The zoo explained that the mother is believed to belong to the third generation of eastern massasaugas descended from a population that may have been the last of its kind in the northern suburbs of Cook County.Importance of this birth for the speciesThe significance of the arrival goes beyond the number of newborns. Lincoln Park Zoo described the young snakes as the great-grandchildren of what are likely Cook County’s last remaining eastern massasaugas. These original snakes were brought to the zoo in 2009 after their wild population faced serious threats from human persecution and habitat loss.The zoo is working alongside state and federal authorities to protect the species, which is often misunderstood because of its venomous bite. Curator Dan Boehm explained that eastern massasaugas are generally shy animals and play an important role in the Great Lakes region's ecosystem.How do eastern massasauga rattlesnakes give birthEastern massasaugas have a reproductive process that differs from that of many other reptiles. According to Lincoln Park Zoo, they are ovoviviparous, meaning their developing young grow inside eggs that remain within the mother's body until they are ready to hatch. The female then gives birth to live young rather than laying eggs in a nest.The gestation period typically lasts around three and a half months. This makes the arrival of the nine young the result of several months of development before they were born.The zoo also noted that maternal protection has been observed in several rattlesnake species. Following the birth, some of the newborn eastern massasaugas were seen staying close to their mother, offering an interesting glimpse into their early behaviour.Unlike adult rattlesnakes, the young do not have fully developed rattles. These structures develop gradually as the snakes grow and shed their skin, with new segments being added over time.A closer look at the snakes and their natural habitatEastern massasauga rattlesnakes are relatively small pit vipers, measuring around 2 feet in length on average. Adults generally have grey or light brown bodies marked with large brown spots along their backs. Younger snakes tend to have more vivid colouring, which helps them blend into the environments where they live.According to Lincoln Park Zoo, the species is found in wetland habitats around the Great Lakes, across parts of the United States and Canada. Its wider range extends east towards New York, west into Iowa and Missouri, and north to southeastern Ontario.These snakes are particularly dependent on wetlands, marshes, fields and prairies. Their natural colouring provides camouflage in these surroundings, helping them remain less visible to predators and other potential threats.Despite being venomous, eastern massasaugas are generally shy and avoid human contact. The zoo has pointed out that encounters with people are uncommon and reported bites are very rare.However, their preference for wetland environments has made them vulnerable to habitat loss. Human activity and the destruction or alteration of these natural areas have contributed to declining populations, making conservation programmes increasingly important.Conservation teams continue to monitor rattlesnake populationsLincoln Park Zoo's breeding success is part of a much wider effort to understand and protect eastern massasaugas. Its February 23 announcement highlighted a long-running research partnership that began in 2009 and involves more than 20 other zoos, the Edward Lowe Foundation, Northern Illinois University and several wildlife agencies.The partnership has focused on studying wild eastern massasauga populations in Michigan. Together, researchers have individually identified more than 900 rattlesnakes and continued monitoring them over the years.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.title: November’s sky has a full supermoon on November 24 that starts a run of three, the Leonid meteor shower peaking before dawn on November 17 and 18, and Taurid showers known for bright fireballs, NASA says
articles.summary: The sky holds mysteries that the most evolved humans have not been able to figure out yet.
articles.body: The sky holds mysteries that the most evolved humans have not been able to figure out yet. The galaxies, moons and celestial bodies withheld in the vastness of the universe depict phenomena that occur only once in a while. An even rarer event is actually witnessing some of these events in the sky. While sleeping under the stars has become a fantasy in the modern world, the sky remains under close observation by the scientists to constantly know more about the world beyond Earth. This November, the universe is offering plenty of reasons to step outside, leave the city lights behind and look up.According to NASA’s November 2026 guide for skywatching, a tempting combination of celestial events are awaiting you. Some of them are the Leonid meteor shower around November 17 and 18, the bright fireballs associated with the Taurid meteor showers, and a full supermoon on November 24.1. The LeonidsBest time: Before dawn on November 17-18, after the Moon sets.If you have ever wanted to make a wish on a shooting star, mark these dates on your calendar. The Leonid meteor shower is expected to offer its best viewing opportunity in the early hours of November 17 and 18. Under ideal dark-sky conditions, observers could see around 15 meteors an hour, although the actual number of meteors visible to anyone may be lower.The Leonids are remnants of Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. As Earth passes through the trail of debris left behind by the comet, tiny particles enter our atmosphere at extraordinary speeds, heating up and creating the bright streaks we call shooting stars. Leonids are particularly speedy, travelling at around 70 kilometres per second.For the best experience, find a spot away from streetlights, settle into a reclining chair and give your eyes about 30 minutes to adjust to the darkness. The Leonids, as the name suggests belong to the constellation Leo.In India, consider a quiet, permitted stargazing spot in Ladakh, Spiti or another low-light destination, checking local weather and access conditions before setting out.2. The TauridsPeak dates: Around November 5 for the Southern Taurids and November 12 for the Northern Taurids.NASA notes that the Southern Taurids peak around November 5, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12. Each typically produces only a handful of meteors per hour under ideal conditions, but the showers are known for occasional bright fireballs. Taurid meteors are associated with relatively large particles, which helps explain their reputation for producing these striking displays.The showers are active across a broader period, so missing their peak dates does not necessarily mean missing every opportunity. If you are travelling in early November, try spending an evening somewhere with an unobstructed view of the sky.3. A supermoonBest time: The evening of November 24, around moonrise.On November 24, a full supermoon will rise, beginning a sequence of three consecutive supermoons spanning November, December and January.A supermoon occurs when a full Moon coincides with a relatively close point in its orbit around Earth. Because the Moon's orbit is elliptical, its distance from us changes over time. When a full Moon occurs closer to Earth than usual, it can appear slightly larger and brighter than an average full Moon.How to plan your own stargazing escapeYou do not need to chase all three events in one trip. Pick the experience that appeals to you most.A few simple preparations can make a significant difference:Escape artificial light. Choose a dark-sky location away from brightly lit roads, hotels and city centres.Check the forecast. Clouds can spoil even the most promising astronomical event.Dress for the night. Temperatures can fall sharply after sunset, particularly in mountain destinations.Bring a chair and a blanket. Meteor watching involves looking at a large portion of the sky, not craning your neck at one small patch.Put your phone away. Bright screens interfere with dark adaptation; if you need an astronomy app, use its red-light setting.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: In 1930, an 11-year-old British girl suggested the name Pluto over breakfast after hearing about a newly discovered planet; astronomers accepted her suggestion, making her part of space history
articles.summary: The discovery of a new planet in 1930 beyond Neptune gave astronomers an unexpected task of finding a suitable name for it.
articles.body: The discovery of a new planet in 1930 beyond Neptune gave astronomers an unexpected task of finding a suitable name for it. Among the many suggestions submitted to the Lowell Observatory in Arizona was one from an 11-year-old British schoolgirl named Venetia Burney. Her idea was inspired by classical mythology and a conversation over breakfast with her grandfather. The observatory eventually selected her suggestion, giving the distant celestial body a name that would remain familiar for decades, even after its classification changed.An 11-year-old British girl came up with the name PlutoThe story began in Oxford, England, where Venetia Burney lived with her family. On 14 March 1930, she was having breakfast with her mother and grandfather, Falconer Madan, when he shared the news that astronomers had discovered a new planet. He wondered what the newly identified object might be called.According to an interview with NASA in January 2006, Burney recalled that she suggested Pluto after a short pause. She was familiar with Greek and Roman mythology through the children's books she had read and already knew the names of the other planets in the solar system. She felt Pluto was a suitable choice because the name had not been used for another planet.The suggestion was not the result of a formal discussion or any involvement in scientific research. It was a simple idea offered during an ordinary family breakfast. However, her grandfather recognised its potential and decided to pass it on to someone who could bring it to the attention of astronomers.The discovery that started the search for a nameThe American Astronomical Society explained that the search for another planet had started years before Burney made her suggestion.American astronomer Percival Lowell had begun searching for an unseen planet beyond Neptune in 1906. He believed that an undiscovered object, which he called Planet X, was influencing the orbits of Uranus and Neptune. Although his search continued until his death in 1916, he did not find the object.The search resumed in 1929 when Vesto Slipher, director of Lowell Observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona, hired Clyde Tombaugh to continue the work. Tombaugh used photographic plates to record sections of the night sky on different nights. By comparing the images, he could identify objects that had moved against the background of distant stars.After months of systematic observations, Tombaugh identified a moving object on photographic plates taken on 23 and 29 January 1930. The discovery was confirmed, and Lowell Observatory announced it on 13 March 1930.The discovery attracted considerable attention because the object appeared to be another world beyond Neptune, making it an important addition to the known solar system.How did the suggestion reach American astronomersBurney's grandfather played an important role in taking the idea beyond the family breakfast table. Falconer Madan was a retired librarian who had previously served as the head librarian at the Bodleian Library at the University of Oxford. He also had connections with several astronomers.As NASA explained in its interview with Burney, Madan passed the proposed name to Herbert Hall Turner, an Oxford professor and former Astronomer Royal. Turner was attending a meeting of the Royal Astronomical Society in London when he received the suggestion.The Arizona Memory Project preserves an important piece of evidence from this exchange. Its digital archive contains a telegram sent by Turner to Lowell Observatory on 16 March 1930, relaying the suggestion of Pluto and identifying Burney as the young English girl who had proposed it.Why did astronomers choose the name PlutoIn Roman mythology, Pluto was the god of the underworld. The name was considered appropriate for a distant, dark and relatively mysterious object located at the outer edges of the solar system. It also maintained the tradition of giving planets names connected with classical mythology.There was another interesting detail. The first two letters of Pluto were the initials of Percival Lowell, whose earlier search for Planet X had helped set the discovery in motion.According to EarthSky, Lowell Observatory received around 1,000 suggestions from people around the world. Despite the large number of entries, Burney's proposal was ultimately selected.The observatory officially announced the name on 1 May 1930. EarthSky also reported that Burney received £5 as a reward for her suggestion.Pluto's place in the solar system changed over timeFor more than 70 years, Pluto was recognised as the 9th planet in the solar system. Its status, however, became a subject of discussion as astronomers discovered more objects in the distant region beyond Neptune.The American Astronomical Society noted that from 1992 onwards, several other bodies were identified orbiting the Sun in the same region as Pluto, now known as the Kuiper Belt. These discoveries led scientists to reconsider whether Pluto fitted the traditional definition of a planet.In 2006, the International Astronomical Union introduced a formal definition of a planet and established a separate category called dwarf planets. Pluto did not meet all the requirements and was placed in the new category. It became the first object recognised in this classification.Although its scientific classification changed, its name remained untouched.How did Venetia Burney's suggestion become part of space historyBurney did not pursue a career in astronomy. According to NASA, she later worked as an accountant and taught economics and mathematics in England. Nevertheless, her contribution continued to attract attention long after the naming decision.NASA interviewed her in 2006, shortly before the launch of the New Horizons spacecraft, which was designed to explore Pluto and the Kuiper Belt. The spacecraft reached Pluto in July 2015, providing the first close-up observations of the distant world.In recognition of Burney's contribution, the New Horizons team renamed its Student Dust Counter instrument the Venetia Burney Student Dust Counter in June 2006. NASA later presented her with a plaque, certificate and spacecraft model during a small ceremony at her home.Burney died on 30 April 2009, aged 90, at her home in Epsom, England.Your child uses AI every day.
