articles.title: Raleigh Museum scientists are opening a 5,000-pound rare ostrich-like dinosaur fossil from Utah in a public lab; this 75-million-year-old fossil could represent a new species if researchers confirm its identity
articles.summary: Scientists at the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences in Raleigh are getting ready to open a 5,000-pound block of sandstone holding a rare,
articles.body: Scientists at the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences in Raleigh are getting ready to open a 5,000-pound block of sandstone holding a rare, ostrich-like dinosaur from Utah. The skeleton is 75 million years old, and it could represent a new species if researchers confirm its identity. The work will take place in the museum's public Dino Lab, so visitors can watch. Crews delivered the block on Wednesday, and Raleigh could now be at the forefront of the discovery of a new dinosaur.What arrived at the museum on Wednesday?Crews delivered the skeleton of a 75-million-year-old dinosaur to the museum on Wednesday, and the staff was happy with how it went. "We're thrilled, we're thrilled, and everything went really well," said Lindsay Zanno, the museum's head of palaeontology.Zanno called it a "really exciting moment" for the museum. "We brought in the coiled-up skeleton of probably a new species of dinosaur," she said. She said "probably", so the dinosaur is not officially a new species yet. That depends on what the researchers find once they start studying it.What did the dinosaur look like?Zanno says the dinosaur would have looked like a large ostrich with a long tail. The skeleton that arrived in Raleigh is coiled up, and she says it is probably complete, with the head wrapped all the way around through the tail.She also spoke highly of the find itself. "This is the most beautiful skeleton of this type of dinosaur that we've ever found in that area," Zanno said.How did it get out of Utah?A scientist who collaborates with the museum discovered the skeleton in southern Utah. Moving it to Raleigh took real effort. Crews had to use a helicopter to lift it out of the desert before the long journey east could start.The size of the block explains why. "It was quite an ordeal," Zanno said. "This ended up being about a 5,000-pound block of sandstone, and that's because the skeleton is probably complete with a head all the way wrapped around through the tail." The skeleton travelled inside the sandstone, and the whole block weighed about 5,000 pounds.Could it really be a new species?That is what the researchers have to find out. Zanno says the skeleton is probably a new species, and the museum's palaeontologists will research it to confirm.If they do confirm it, Raleigh could be at the forefront of the discovery. For now, it is a strong possibility and nothing more. The report does not say how long the research will take or how the scientists will go about it. It only says the work will happen at the museum, where the skeleton now sits.Where will the fossil be opened?Palaeontologists will research the skeleton inside the museum's State Employees' Credit Union (SECU) Dino Lab. The lab opened a few years ago so scientists could study the duelling dinosaurs, which Zanno says everyone knows and loves.She described the new skeleton as the next step in that work. "It's just following along with what we built here at the North Carolina museum a few years ago when we opened the new dino lab," she said. "We did that to study the duelling dinosaurs, which everyone knows and loves, but this is sort of the next phase of what's going to take place at the museum."Can the public watch?Yes. The Dino Lab is part of the museum's free admission, so visitors can see researchers work on the new dinosaur. They can also see the researchers work on other dinosaurs in the lab.That means people in Raleigh will not have to wait for a published paper to learn what is inside the sandstone. They can walk into the lab and watch the scientists doing the work.What next?The block is in Raleigh now, and the next move belongs to the scientists. They will study a rare, ostrich-like dinosaur that spent 75 million years in the rock before a helicopter lifted it out of the Utah desert.If they confirm that it is a new species, the discovery will be tied to the Dino Lab and the museum that housed it. If they do not, the skeleton is still, in Zanno's words, the most beautiful of its type found in that area.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.title: A Caltech robot launched into orbit in March has assembled part of a space structure without astronauts for the first time, joining individual struts and joints into a new section of an experimental antenna
articles.summary: A robot developed by researchers at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) has successfully assembled part of a structure in space without
articles.body: A robot developed by researchers at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) has successfully assembled part of a structure in space without astronauts carrying out the construction. Launched into orbit in March 2026, the robotic system joined individual components to build a section of an experimental antenna, demonstrating how future space structures could be constructed beyond Earth.The demonstration is part of the US Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency's (DARPA) Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials and Mass-efficient Design (NOM4D) programme. According to DARPA's announcement, the Caltech payload used a robotic system to connect composite truss members with specially designed joints while deploying a thin reflective mesh. The experiment marks a significant step towards building large structures directly in orbit.The project could eventually change how scientists and engineers design space-based antennas, solar arrays and other large installations. Instead of transporting a fully assembled structure from Earth, future missions could carry individual building components and put them together in space. How did the robot complete this task, and what could its success mean for future space exploration?How did the Caltech robot assemble a structure in space?The robotic system, known as the Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly (ASTRA), was designed to build a truss structure using individual components stored inside its payload. It uses an autonomous manipulator that collects struts and joints from nearby dispensers and connects them to create sections, also called bays.The process resembles assembling a construction toy such as K'Nex or Tinkertoys. Individual members fit together at connecting points, allowing the robot to build a larger structure one section at a time. Once a section is assembled, the system attaches a thin, net-like reflective surface to it.The experimental antenna was designed to measure 1.4 metres in diameter and used composite fibre tubes, aluminium joints and a reflective Kapton surface. The robotic system successfully constructed an additional section of the truss while operating in orbit.Sergio Pellegrino, Caltech's team leader for the ASTRA demonstration, described the achievement as a first. “This is the first time that a structure has been autonomously constructed in space,” he said, according to Phys.org's report on the Caltech project.The demonstration did not require astronauts to assemble the structure manually. However, the research team on Earth sent commands to the onboard computer and examined photographs transmitted from the payload to check the results.Why is assembling structures in space important?Building large structures in space presents a practical challenge. Rockets have limited room for cargo, which restricts the size of objects that can travel inside them. Engineers have traditionally addressed this problem by folding structures before launch and unfolding them after reaching orbit, or by sending large components through multiple launches and assembling them manually.Both approaches place limits on the size and complexity of future installations. Building structures directly in space could offer another way to overcome these restrictions.DARPA's NOM4D programme aims to develop methods for constructing very large structures beyond Earth. Andrew Detor, the programme's manager, said its objective was to enable construction on a scale that could eventually reach hundreds of metres or even kilometres. Such structures are beyond what current construction methods can achieve.The approach could support future space-based radio antennas, large solar arrays and habitats. Scientists could also use enormous reflector surfaces to build powerful space telescopes capable of observing distant objects.Detor compared the Caltech system to construction toys, explaining that it joins individual truss members at connecting points to create a larger structure. He also noted that the system combines several operations in a way that could make the process scalable.How did the robot operate after its launch?The ASTRA payload travelled to low Earth orbit aboard SpaceX's Transporter-16 mission on March 30, 2026. Momentus supported the mission by hosting the payload on its Vigoride orbital vehicle and providing services such as communications, power and imaging.The payload carried two preassembled sections of the truss, along with a robotic manipulator and the components needed to build another section. After reaching orbit, the team released the launch restraints and deployed the two prebuilt sections. The robot then began assembling the next section using components stored in motorised dispensers.The process required careful coordination between the researchers on Earth and the system in orbit. Team members sent commands to the onboard computer and checked images returned by the payload. When unexpected problems appeared, engineers tested possible solutions using a spare version of the system in Caltech's laboratory before sending instructions to the flight unit.Communication also presented a challenge. Researchers had only around seven or eight short communication windows of approximately 15 minutes each day to contact the system. This meant the team had to identify problems, test solutions and relay instructions within limited periods. The researchers faced time constraints and could not complete the entire antenna structure. However, the robot successfully built the initial section needed to demonstrate that the assembly approach could work in the space environment.What could this technology mean for future space missions?The ASTRA demonstration is a proof of concept rather than a finished construction system. The team has shown that a robot can assemble structural components in orbit, but engineers still need to simplify and refine the design before applying the technology to much larger projects. The experiment also revealed why testing in space matters. Conditions beyond Earth differ significantly from those in a laboratory, and unexpected problems can affect how robotic systems operate. The researchers used the mission to understand these challenges and identify improvements for future versions.Pellegrino said the demonstration had opened new possibilities for research. The technology could eventually help construct large reflector surfaces for astronomy, communications systems and space-based solar power installations.DARPA's NOM4D programme has another milestone planned. A team from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign is expected to test a different space-manufacturing approach aboard the International Space Station. Its project will examine how a specially developed resin system can be processed in space to produce a high-strength composite structure.The Caltech experiment has not yet delivered the enormous structures that future missions may require. It has, however, demonstrated a possible way to build beyond the size limits imposed by rocket launches. As space agencies and researchers explore longer-term missions, automated construction could help turn ambitious designs into structures assembled directly where they are needed.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Exclusive: China dominates battery graphite, but this startup could break the monopoly | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Chinese companies maintain near total dominance of the graphite industry, but Molten Industries says its new factory in Oakland could spell the end of the monopoly.
articles.body:
Electric vehicle sales in the U.S. may have leveled off, but the market for batteries inside them isn’t slowing down, quintupling in the last five years. Many of those are made in the U.S., but they’re largely dependent on China for key ingredients, including graphite.

Graphite is a key ingredient in lithium-ion batteries, where it forms the anode, the part that stores the battery’s charge. Chinese companies control about three-quarters of the graphite anode supply chain and 97% of synthetic (human-made) graphite anode production, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence . One five-year-old startup, Molten Industries , is working to break that dominance.

Molten Industries has started operating a demonstration plant in Oakland meant to prove the technology works, the company exclusively told TechCrunch. The plant is will pave the way for U.S.-made graphite to win a share of the market.

“The new plant will be producing graphite that’s at cost parity with China plus tariffs,” Caleb Boyd, co-founder and CTO of Molten Industries, told TechCrunch. In other words, once U.S. import taxes are added to Chinese graphite, Molten’s price would match it. He said future plants should match China’s cost even without tariffs, which he called a built-in advantage of the technology.

Molten’s Oakland plant will make about 300 metric tons of graphite annually, which is enough for 300 megawatt-hours of batteries. That’s enough for about 4,300 EVs. The bulk of the output will go to undisclosed customers that are testing it in their battery cells.

The next facility, which Molten has yet to announce, will take the same template used in the Oakland plant and replicate it several times over, said Boyd.

The startup’s technology began in a Silicon Valley garage . It uses electrical resistive heating, which passes electricity through a material to heat it, to split methane (the main ingredient in natural gas) into pure carbon and hydrogen. “You can think of it almost like a massive toaster,” Boyd said. The company says the system uses three times less electricity than existing methods, and it runs on natural gas, which is cheap and plentiful in the U.S.

“We think it’s very hard to compete with China if you’re just copying their processes and trying to compete on cost,” said Kevin Bush, who co-founded Molten Industries with Boyd and is the company’s CEO. “So we are using a resource in the United States that’s abundant in natural gas, and we’ve brought some innovation to actually be able to drive down the cost of graphite production globally.”

Here’s how the chemistry works: When methane (CH4) is heated without oxygen, each molecule breaks into one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. The hydrogen atoms pair up into hydrogen gas (H2), which Molten sells at market prices to a customer next door. The carbon is then processed to meet battery makers’ requirements.

The basic idea of using heat to separate methane has been around for over a century, but early attempts to commercialize it ran into trouble. Carbon built up and clogged the reactor, and Boyd said no company before Molten had been able to produce high-quality graphite this way.

Solving that problem changed the company’s direction. Boyd and Bush — both materials science PhDs from Stanford — originally set out to make clean hydrogen from natural gas. Most hydrogen today comes from steam reforming, a cheap but polluting process. The two wanted to reap the benefits of a low-cost feedstock like natural gas without the pollution, and they expected to sell the leftover carbon as a by-product.

But as they experimented with ways to keep the reactor clean, “we actually started making this really high-quality graphite,” Boyd said, which “changed the entire economics of what we were doing.” Molten went from a hydrogen company that happened to sell graphite to a battery-grade graphite company that happens to sell hydrogen.

The company says both businesses could bring in billions of dollars. If Molten supplied the entire U.S. battery market, it could also provide about a third of the hydrogen used in the country, the company claims. Other uses for high-quality graphite, like thermal batteries that store energy as heat, could expand both markets further.

The new factory, Boyd said, “is really a milestone, not just for the company, we think, but globally.”

articles.title: 200,000 walruses are forced ashore in Alaska as sea ice melts. Now there’s a plan to protect them
articles.summary: Nearly 50,000 acres in northwest Alaska is now a permanently protected refuge for Pacific walruses as they struggle to adapt to the loss of their sea ice hab...
articles.body:
The Pacific walrus haulout in northwest Alaska is something to behold. Every fall, more than 200,000 walruses heave themselves onto the barrier islands near the village of Point Lay, forming an undulating mass of brownish-pink blubber and white tusks with not an inch between their bodies. The noise is deafening; the smell is overpowering.

"It's this cacophony of life… it is overwhelming to the senses," said John Wros, Alaska state director at the Conservation Fund, an environmental non-profit. "There's a lot of energy; there are animals that are playing in the surf."

The dramatic gathering looks joyful, but it tells the story of a species forced to adapt to the impacts of climate change in real time. For the last two decades, the sea ice the walruses depend on has disappeared, driving them to seek refuge on this slice of land on the shore of the vast Chukchi Sea, which stretches between northern Alaska and Russia's Siberian coast.

"This is an example of animals responding to change, but it does not mean that land can fully replace the habitat they are losing," said said Chelsea Koch, a marine scientist at American University.

On Wednesday, the Conservation Fund announced a plan to secure nearly 50,000 acres of this land, including the barrier islands, as a permanent refuge for the walruses.

🧊 Get your local forecast from the CNN Weather app .

The non-profit has signed an agreement with the Cully Corporation, the Alaskan Native Village Corporation that owns the land, to shield the walruses from human activities, including preventing resource development.

In exchange, the Cully Corporation receives a payment aimed at boosting financial security and protecting the way of life of local communities, whose relationship with walruses, in terms of food and culture, spans thousands of years.

"Big animals need even bigger landscapes to thrive, and the Pacific walrus is no exception," said Larry Selzer, president and CEO of The Conservation Fund. This conservation model is "really powerful tool," he added, because it allows them to work with the landowner to ensure the land can still be used for economic purposes while also protecting crucial wildlife habitats.

Willard Neakok, chairman of the Cully Corporation Board, said the partnership will create opportunities and help preserve Inupiaq heritage. "We respect our land, we respect our tradition, history, culture. So we're doing this for future descendants," he said.

The population of Pacific walruses has been relatively stable, but they are experiencing "a new normal" of disappearing sea ice and it's a threat, said Anthony Fischbach, a wildlife biologist at the US Geological Survey.

Pacific walruses spend their winters on the pack ice of the Bering Sea. While the males remain there year-round, the females and their young migrate north to feed on the shallow shoals of the Chukchi Sea.

Historically they relied on persistent Arctic sea ice as platforms to rest near feeding grounds, to give birth and to nurse their young. But, as humans burn fossil fuels and heat the planet, that sea ice has gone.

"In late summer, the ice now often retreats beyond the shallow continental shelf into waters too deep for walruses to feed on the seafloor," Koch said.

Without ice, the walruses are increasingly forced to turn to solid land. Hauling out on land is not unheard of, but the enormous numbers that now gather at Point Lay is something new.

It started in 2007, with a few thousand females and their calves, but the numbers cranked up quickly. Now almost all Pacific walrus females and their young — around 200,000 in total — use the site. It's the largest haulout in North America, Wros said.

"They're seeking a refuge on land; this is a fundamental change" and it's a direct result of climate change, he said.

In one sense, this remarkable phenomenon is a testament to walruses' ability to adapt. But gatherings of this size can be dangerous.

A harrowing scene in the 2019 Netflix documentary "Our Planet" helped sear this into the public consciousness. Hundreds of walruses that had climbed up cliffs overlooking a Russian beach to escape the crush below were filmed falling off the edge , their huge bodies tumbling 260 feet to the jagged rocks below.

At Point Lay, the big danger is stampedes. Walruses are easily spooked and even small disturbances can cause these huge animals — which can weigh up to 2 tons — to flee toward the ocean. "There are these mass die-off events where juveniles are crushed and killed by the hundreds, if not thousands," Wros said.

Sometimes it's a polar bear that startles them, but often it's human caused — an airplane that flies too low, ship traffic and even tourists on cruises keen to spot the animals.

Point Lay also sits on the edge of the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska, an area in the crosshairs of resource development, including for fossil fuels.

The new conservation agreement aims to restrict disturbances from commercial activities and tourism, while at the same time ensuring residents have access to the natural resources they need to meet their needs, as well as financial resources so they aren't forced to sell land for oil and gas development.

"It's a big step for village elders to say 'we're going to permanently give up certain rights'," Selzer said. It took time to build trust, he added, which is why the project was 10 years in the making.

The Conservation Fund has not revealed the amount paid to the Cully Corporation.

American University's Koch did not comment specifically on the Point Lay plan but she sees "promise in conservation approaches that support local stewardship, while protecting important walrus habitat," she said.

Whether this kind of conservation arrangement might also work elsewhere would depend on the community, Koch added. "My main questions would be whether residents are shaping the decisions, whether subsistence rights and access are protected and whether there is lasting support for local monitoring and stewardship."

As sea ice continues its downward spiral, Wros hopes this new refuge will give walruses a fighting chance.

"The damage has been done, and this is adaptation in real time," he said. "This is what we're choosing to do about it to ensure that those animals can persist."

articles.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is now 1 light-day away
articles.summary: After traveling through the void of space for 49 years, Voyager 1 has hit a momentous milestone: the spacecraft is now officially one light-day away from Earth.
articles.body: After traveling through the void of space for 49 years, Voyager 1 has hit a momentous milestone: The spacecraft is now officially 1 light-day away from Earth, which is, as NASA put it, “very, very far.” The probe crossed the milepost on Wednesday at 5:16AM ET and is now 16.094 billion miles away from our planet — equal to the distance that light travels in 24 hours. It’s the farthest that any human-made object has ever traveled, and Voyager 1’s journey isn’t over yet. It’s been heading toward a star called Gliese 445 in the Ursa Minor constellation since completing its primary objectives to conduct flybys of Jupiter and Saturn in 1980. That star is 17 light-years away, meaning Voyager 1 won’t pass by it for around 40,000 years, despite traveling at nearly 38,000 mph. [Media: The light-day milestone is a remarkable feat alone, but especially so when you consider that Voyager 1 is still operational. NASA has done well to keep it functioning, and it can continue to send back readings on plasma waves, magnetic fields, and space-bound particles, though it now takes radio signals an entire day to travel between Earth and the spacecraft. Voyager 2, which launched 16 days before its twin, is also expected to reach a distance of 1 light-day away from Earth, but not until 2035.

articles.title: MIT engineers copied the branching patterns of leaves and dragonfly wings to 3D-print small protective structures; in laboratory tests, the uneven networks absorbed impacts better than conventional honeycomb designs
articles.summary: The world around us is built on patterns and networks that often resemble one another. For instance, consider a honeycomb.
articles.body: The world around us is built on patterns and networks that often resemble one another. For instance, consider a honeycomb. If you look closely, you will notice a consistent pattern running through its internal structure, made up of repeating hexagonal shapes. But does this repetitive arrangement affect the material's resilience? Engineers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), USA, have now set out to explore this question.According to MIT News, in a report dated November 11, 2026, engineers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and Northeastern University have developed a new kind of material whose internal structure is deliberately varied rather than built from one repeating design. This approach could eventually inform the design of protective equipment and packaging.The researchers have introduced what they call "scale-rich metamaterials". Metamaterials are engineered materials whose properties are shaped not only by what they are made of but also by how their internal structures are arranged. Instead of relying on a single building block repeated across the material, the new design brings together a network of beams that vary in length, thickness and the number of connections they make.The findings of the study were published in Nature on November 11, 2026, in a paper titled "Scale-Rich Network-Based Metamaterials". The study also reports that these structures can be designed to control properties such as stiffness and the way they respond to force.What the research entailed The researchers draw on network science, a field that examines how different points and connections form systems, from the internet and social networks to biological networks in nature. Leaf veins and the veins in dragonfly wings provided examples of intricate natural networks, although the researchers did not simply reproduce the shape of a leaf or wing.Using network principles and an algorithm, the researchers generated a new pattern. It starts by placing a point at a random position and drawing a line through it at a random angle. As more lines are added at different positions and angles, each line stops when it reaches the boundary of the material or intersects an existing line. As this process continues, the lines become progressively shorter and thinner, eventually creating a dense network with features of different sizes.The team then used 3D-printing methods to turn these computer-generated designs into physical samples. According to the MIT report, the researchers deposited polymer in patterns of tiny, interconnected beams. The resulting square samples were approximately the size of a credit card, with internal structures ranging from micrometres to centimetres in scale.The researchers compared the printed materials with conventional lattice and honeycomb metamaterials. They compressed the samples with increasing force and also dropped a heavy weight onto them, recording how each structure responded. The scale-rich networks performed better at resisting compression and impacts in these tests, while their varied internal arrangements helped distribute damage more effectively rather than allowing it to concentrate in one particular region.As MIT mechanical engineering professor Carlos Portela explained, the different sizes of the beams allow the surrounding network to support a structure even if one part fails.A protective layer inspired by a fruitThe researchers also explored whether this arrangement could be modified to protect something fragile inside a material. In search of an answer, they looked to the pomelo, a citrus fruit known for its thick rind and the variation in density between its outer and inner layers. Inspired by this structure, the team designed a material with a denser network of beams around its edges. A fragile object was placed at the centre, and the researchers tested how well the surrounding structure could shield it. Their design helped divert forces away from the object, showcasing how the density and arrangement of a network could be adjusted depending on what needed protection.What this could mean for everyday materialsThe applications of this research could include objects that need to cushion sudden impacts, such as helmets, protective gear, packaging and armour. The same design framework could also be useful in acoustic lenses, which guide or focus sound and vibrations.However, these possibilities should be understood as potential applications rather than products already ready for everyday use. The findings come from computer modelling and controlled laboratory experiments on engineered samples. Therefore, further research will be needed to determine how these findings could take shape in everyday materials.The study has brought a rather gripping insight, turning an apparent lack of order into a design advantage. Nature's networks are rarely made up of uniform or repetitive connections, but learning from the myriad structures found in rinds, leaves and wings has brought a new possibility into the field of innovation: exploring how materials can become more resilient without having to make every part of them uniform.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: A $114 million wildlife bridge over California's 101 freeway has recorded a coyote believed to have made the first full crossing before its December 2 opening; the project spans 1,250 feet and reconnects habitat divided by 300,000 cars a day
articles.summary: A coyote has been recorded using a new wildlife bridge over California's busy US 101 Freeway, offering an early sign that the structure could help animals
articles.body: A coyote has been recorded using a new wildlife bridge over California's busy US 101 Freeway, offering an early sign that the structure could help animals move safely between habitats. The $114 million Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing in Agoura Hills is designed to reconnect natural areas separated by the highway and surrounding development. In a November 4, 2026 announcement, the National Park Service (NPS) reported the first photograph of a coyote climbing the unfinished crossing and confirmed that the structure is scheduled to open to wildlife on December 2.Stretching 1,250 feet across the freeway and an adjoining road, the bridge provides a route between the Santa Monica Mountains and the Simi Hills. Around 300,000 vehicles travel along this section of the 101 every day, making it a significant barrier for animals moving through the region.How the first coyote was spottedThe first coyote photograph was captured on October 28 by a National Park Service camera. It showed the animal climbing the southern slope of the unfinished crossing near Liberty Canyon. The sighting came as scientists were preparing to install remote cameras to monitor how wildlife responds to the new connection.A further coyote sighting was subsequently recorded on the upper section of the structure. Early reports said researchers could not establish whether the animal had completed the entire crossing, as construction was still under way.An Associated Press report published on November 18 provided a later update, saying motion-sensor cameras had captured a lone coyote believed to be the first mammal to make the full crossing. The report also noted that three young coyotes had been filmed playing in vegetation beneath the sound-dampening walls along the structure.Why the wildlife bridge mattersThe highway has divided habitats used by animals in the Santa Monica Mountains and surrounding areas for decades. Roads and urban development have restricted their movement, making it harder for wildlife to find food, shelter and potential mates.Mountain lions are among the species conservationists particularly hope will benefit. Isolated populations can face limited opportunities to breed with unrelated animals, increasing the risk of inbreeding and reducing genetic diversity. A safer route between habitats could allow these animals to move across a wider area and connect with other populations.The crossing is also expected to benefit coyotes, bobcats, gray foxes and mule deer. Its surface is being covered with soil and native vegetation to make it resemble the surrounding hillsides. Fencing along the freeway will help guide animals towards the overpass rather than allowing them to enter traffic.How scientists will monitor wildlife activityThe National Park Service and its partners are using remote cameras to record which species approach and use the structure, as well as when they cross. The monitoring programme will help researchers assess whether the bridge is improving habitat connectivity and how different animals respond to the new route.Before the crossing is fully open, scientists had already observed bobcats, coyotes, gray foxes, mule deer and mountain lions using a trail near the construction site. Researchers will continue studying animal movement through camera monitoring, GPS tracking and other scientific methods.The findings will help establish whether the crossing is being used regularly and whether it is helping wildlife populations move between previously separated areas.A major investment in conservationThe project is being developed through a partnership involving the National Wildlife Federation, the Mountains Recreation and Conservation Authority, Caltrans and the National Park Service. Its total cost has reached approximately $114 million, supported by public funding, grants and private donations. The late philanthropist Wallis Annenberg's foundation contributed $25 million, and the crossing was named in her honour. The project faced construction challenges, including heavy rainfall and flooding in earlier years, which affected progress. It is now approaching its planned December 2 opening.For conservationists, the early animal sightings are an encouraging development. However, the long-term success of the crossing will depend on whether wildlife continues to use it, particularly mountain lions whose survival can depend on access to larger, connected habitats.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Carrion crows can decide which way a cloud of dots was moving in about 235 milliseconds, roughly twice as fast as humans and monkeys, scientists at Germany’s University of Tübingen report
articles.summary: What goes through an animal's mind when it sees something moving in front of it?
articles.body: What goes through an animal's mind when it sees something moving in front of it? Whether it is a bird spotting a potential meal, trying to avoid an obstacle while flying, or simply following the movement of another animal, its visual processing and ability to assess what it sees are crucial for making decisions about prey and possible threats. Sometimes, the difference between responding in time and missing an opportunity by a moment comes down to a fraction of a second.Researchers studying carrion crows have found that these birds make visual decisions at roughly twice the speed previously observed in humans and monkeys, taking just 235 milliseconds on average. This is a remarkable speed, particularly when compared with the time humans and other primates typically take to complete similar tasks.The findings come from a study published in the journal Science on October 22, 2026, titled "Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain." Researchers Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder from the Institute of Neurobiology at the University of Tübingen in Germany investigated how quickly carrion crows could interpret visual information and make a decision based on what they saw.A simple task that required a quick decisionTo understand how the experiment worked and what the researchers concluded, first, imagine looking at a screen with dots in motion and being asked to decide which direction most of these dots are travelling towards: left or right? While the question is rather direct and simple, discerning the precise movement of the dots, let alone understanding the full pattern of their movement, can be quite a task. But this is essentially what the researchers asked the crows to do.The experiment involved two male carrion crows (Corvus corone) that were presented with moving dots on a touchscreen and had to determine whether the majority of the dots were moving towards the left or right. They indicated their response by pecking at a target on the corresponding side of the screen. The researchers also varied how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction, making some patterns easier to interpret than others. When the direction was relatively clear, the birds were not only remarkably quick but also accurate. Even when the patterns were more difficult to distinguish, their decisions were better than a random guess.What happens inside a crow's brain?But the researchers were interested in more than simply finding out how quickly the birds could complete the task. They also wanted to comprehend what was really happening in the birds' brains and how they arrived at their decisions. Therefore, to investigate this, the team recorded the activity of individual neurons in a region of the crow's brain known as the nidopallium caudolaterale, which plays an important role in information processing and decision-making.One of the more fascinating findings was that the researchers could identify signals associated with the birds' eventual choices just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared on the screen. This was nearly 170 milliseconds before the birds even physically responded by pecking at their chosen target. To put it simply, their brains seemed to already be showing signs of which direction the crows would select long before the birds made their responses visible.As the birds continued to assess the pattern, the activity of the brain neurons was just as fascinating, as it gradually increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. When the visual evidence was stronger, the birds had more information to work with, allowing their brains to arrive at a choice.This process of decision-making has already been observed in humans and other primates, where the brain gradually gathers sensory information before reaching a particular threshold and settling on a choice.Quick decision-makingBirds and mammals have evolved very different brain structures, and one of the distinctions is that birds do not possess the same layered cerebral cortex found in mammals. The findings suggest that, despite their structural differences, birds and primates can rely on comparable underlying processes when it comes to making decisions.According to Professor Andreas Nieder, the neuronal activity observed in the crows was consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates. The difference, however, was the remarkable speed at which the birds completed the task.These findings reveal to us that perhaps a lot more fast-paced thinking is happening behind those watchful eyes than science had previously asserted. And while scientists still have questions about exactly how the crow's brain achieves this speed, the study adds another interesting piece to our understanding of how very different animal brains can arrive at surprisingly similar decisions, even if the speed may differ.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: A milestone for NASA’s Voyager 1 probe: a distance of one ‘light-day’ from Earth
articles.summary: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is believed to have hit a distance milestone accomplished by no other spacecraft from Earth: one light-day, or the distance that light travels in 24 hours.
articles.body: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is believed to have now hit a distance milestone accomplished by no other spacecraft from Earth, based on advance computations by the US space agency, as the probe ventures through the near-emptiness of interstellar space. The robotic probe, launched in 1977, was calculated by NASA to have reached a light-day from Earth, the distance that light travels in 24 hours — about 16 billion miles — on Wednesday at 5:16 a.m. ET. Officials at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California will have to wait about a day to get a signal from the probe, confirming it has reached this distance. They have scheduled an event for Thursday to discuss the milestone. “Reaching one light-day is an astounding feat, one that I never expected to see,” Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd said. Voyager 1, the most distant human-made object, is flying at almost 38,000 miles per hour. It crossed the outer edge of the heliosphere, a protective bubble of particles and magnetic fields produced by the sun, to enter ‌interstellar space ⁠in 2012. Its twin, Voyager 2, was also launched in 1977 and entered interstellar space in 2018. A Jet Propulsion Laboratory representative said recent power-saving measures could give the two Voyager spacecraft enough power to stay in communication with Earth for three to four more years. “But the goal of the mission is to do science, and there is enough power to keep the current suite of instruments going through the 50th launch anniversary next year. Beyond that is hard to predict, and of course these are nearly 50-year-old spacecraft, and there are always things the team cannot anticipate that might happen,” the JPL representative said. Voyager 1 journeyed past Jupiter and Saturn, the solar system’s two largest planets, earlier in its mission. It continues to gather scientific data. For instance, its instruments have detected the faint monotonous hum caused by the constant vibrations of the small amounts of gas present in interstellar space. “Voyager is sending back continuous measurements of magnetic fields, cosmic rays and of plasma waves that we receive on Earth whenever the Deep Space Network points its antenna at Voyager,” Dodd said. The Deep Space Network is NASA’s international array of giant radio antennas supporting interplanetary spacecraft missions. “After the heliopause crossing, the magnetic field direction did not rotate into the interstellar direction as expected, but has maintained the direction it had when both Voyagers crossed the heliopause, a direction governed by our sun. We are watching to see when that rotation might occur,” Dodd said. “We also are still observing effects from our sun, including strong solar storms like coronal mass ejections, that generate shocks and pressure fronts that reach as far away as Voyager 1 and beyond,” Dodd said. “Where does the sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may last long enough to answer that question.”

articles.title: Las bolas de dragón existen y no son las de Goku: una investigación descubre un molusco que alberga miles de bacterias y las mantiene vivas
articles.standfirst: Esta especie se encontró en las profundidades del mar de China Meridional
articles.summary: Esta especie se encontró en las profundidades del mar de China Meridional
articles.body: Si hablamos de las bolas de dragón, a la mayoría se le podría venir a la cabeza Goku, Piccolo y una serie que marcó a generaciones. No obstante, este nombre tiene una relación con la ciencia mayor de la que podría pensar un ciudadano alejado de esta industria. En el mar de China Meridional, se ha encontrado una especie con el intestino destrozado por completo. Este animal tiene forma de gusano, con una enorme glándula en la que residen cientos de bacterias. Permanece la mayoría del tiempo bajo el lado, así que el oxígeno es prácticamente inexistente. Es por eso que esta especie se ayuda de estas bacterias para sobrevivir. Éstas, a su vez, se encuentran envueltas en pequeñas cápsulas. Pues bien, los investigadores de dicha especie han decidido llamar a estas pequeñas cubiertas ‘bolas de dragón’. No es que los científicos responsables sean muy seguidores de la series de Goku, sino que el nombre de la especie es ‘gusano dragón divino’. De ahí que se emplee esta denominación. Para la ciencia, este gusano no es más que un primo lejano de los caracoles o las almejas. La principal diferencia con ellos es el tamaño que pueden alcanzar los dragones divinos. Si los moluscos suelen ser diminutos, este alcanza de media unos 15 centímetros. Los científicos, por primera vez, los encontraron enterrados a decenas de centímetros bajo el sedimento. Por eso no entendían cómo podían sobrevivir tanto tiempo en esta posición sin oxígeno. Para entenderlo de un modo más sencillo, los investigadores descubrieron que estas bacterias son capaces de obtener energía de los compuestos de azufre que encuentran en el sedimento que rodea al molusco. Es decir, el molusco utiliza a las bacterias como si fuese un equipo de cocineros que le ayuda a convertir estos compuestos en su alimento.

articles.title: Psychology says a few minutes of your speech may reveal how fast your brain is aging, after a model tested on 2,928 Spanish speakers linked bigger gaps between voice age and real age to dementia
articles.summary: Does it irk you when a friend or family member takes several pauses while telling you a story, struggles to find the right word or fills every other
articles.body: Does it irk you when a friend or family member takes several pauses while telling you a story, struggles to find the right word or fills every other sentence with an 'um' or an 'uh'? Well, before you lose your patience, there may be more to these little speech habits than meets the ear.Scientists have developed a new tool called a speech clock, which analyses subtle characteristics of a person's speech to estimate how quickly they are aging. In a study involving 2,928 Spanish-speaking participants across five Latin American countries, researchers found that differences between a person's actual age and their speech-predicted age were associated with cognitive impairment and dementia. The research, published in Science Advances, suggests that the way we speak could offer valuable clues about what is happening inside our brains.What is biological age?Most of us are familiar with chronological age, which is simply the number of years we have been alive. Biological age, however, is a little more complicated. It refers to how old our bodies and biological systems appear to be based on factors such as cellular damage, changes in organs and the effects of aging. The two do not always go hand in hand. Someone who is 60 years old, for instance, may have a biological age considerably younger or older than 60, depending on how their body has aged.Scientists use different kinds of biological clocks to estimate this gap. Some rely on blood samples, DNA changes and molecular markers, while others use brain scans to examine changes in brain structure and functioning.The new research introduces another possibility: using speech as an indicator of biological aging. The researchers call the difference between a person's chronological age and their speech-predicted age the 'speech age gap' (SAG). A positive gap suggests that their speech displays characteristics associated with an older age than their actual age.What did the researchers do?The research team analysed speech recordings from 2,928 participants in Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Peru. The group included 1,504 healthy individuals and 1,424 people with different forms of cognitive impairment, including mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia.Using machine-learning models, the researchers examined hundreds of acoustic and linguistic characteristics in the recordings. These included speech timing, pitch, vocabulary, word choice, the complexity of language, emotional expression and the number of words used.The model was then trained to predict a person's chronological age based on these speech patterns. Researchers compared this predicted age with the participant's actual age to calculate their speech age gap.They also compared the results with existing measures of brain ageing, blood-based biomarkers and cognitive assessments to understand whether the speech clock was picking up meaningful signs of ageing.Main findings of the researchThe results revealed a noticeable difference between healthy participants and those living with cognitive impairment. Healthy individuals generally had smaller speech age gaps, while participants with mild cognitive impairment and dementia tended to have larger ones.The differences were particularly pronounced among people with frontotemporal dementia, especially those whose condition affected language-related abilities. Participants with Alzheimer's disease also showed larger gaps than those with mild cognitive impairment.The researchers further found that larger speech age gaps were associated with poorer performance in several cognitive assessments, including tests measuring executive functioning, memory and overall cognitive ability.There was another interesting finding. Among participants with Alzheimer's disease, larger speech age gaps were associated with higher levels of p-tau217, a protein in the blood linked to Alzheimer's-related brain changes. This suggests that speech patterns may reflect biological changes associated with the disease, rather than simply differences in how people communicate.Interestingly, pitch and emotional content were among the strongest contributors to speech profiles predicted to be older. Meanwhile, speech timing and the number of words used were important in identifying profiles associated with younger predicted ages.What does this mean for future testing?Using a speech clock could offer a relatively low-cost, low-effort way of monitoring aspects of cognitive ageing. Many existing biological ageing models require complicated procedures such as MRI scans, blood samples, molecular tests or specialised clinical assessments.Speech analysis, on the other hand, could be considerably easier to carry out. Recordings can potentially be collected in different settings, processed remotely and repeated over time to monitor changes. It is also non-invasive, making it a potentially more comfortable option for individuals undergoing repeated assessments.This could be particularly useful in regions where advanced diagnostic facilities are difficult to access. A speech-based tool may eventually help researchers identify people who could benefit from further cognitive assessments, without requiring expensive equipment at the first stage.However, it is important to remember that the technology is still being developed. Its purpose would be to complement existing diagnostic methods, not replace them.Limits of the studyHowever, this study, like any other, comes with its own limitations and needs further development. While the results are promising, the research was conducted at a single point in time. This means it cannot establish whether changes in speech appeared before cognitive decline or developed alongside an existing condition.Long-term studies will be needed to determine whether speech clocks can reliably predict future dementia or other age-related conditions.The study also focused on Spanish-speaking participants from five Latin American countries. There is no guarantee that the same model will work equally well across different languages, cultures, accents and speech patterns. Education, social background and recording conditions can also influence how people communicate.And last but not least, a speech clock cannot independently diagnose dementia. Its findings would need to be considered alongside clinical assessments, cognitive tests and, where appropriate, blood biomarkers and brain imaging.Your next long-winded conversation may require a little more patience. While a few awkward pauses are hardly cause for alarm, researchers are beginning to discover that the way we speak could tell us something about how our brains age.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: US-led astronomers found an object that sent two radio pulses every 62.2 minutes during a 15-hour burst in 2022 and then went silent; new research suggests signals came from opposite magnetic regions
articles.summary: Space is a mysterious phenomenon that scientists have been trying to decrypt for a long time.
articles.body: Space is a mysterious phenomenon that scientists have been trying to decrypt for a long time. From an observation as simple as Earth being round to defining the complicated spectacle of a black hole, scientists have made great progress in their mission. But, the vastness of space often presents a novel phenomenon that becomes a challenge for them to define. This happened when astronomers discovered an unusual cosmic object that sent out two powerful radio pulses at regular intervals for about 15 hours and couldn’t be detected for five years after that.That is LPT J1555−5631, the latest entry in one of astronomy's strangest new rogues' galleries.An accidental discoveryAstronomer Scott Hyman of Sweet Briar College wasn't looking for this object. According to ScienceAlert's report, he was hunting for millisecond pulsars which are rapidly spinning dead stars that might explain an excess of gamma rays near the Milky Way's centre.One candidate in MeerKAT archive data behaved oddly, with its "pulses" arriving many minutes apart at suspiciously regular intervals. Another telescope, ASKAP, was watching the same patch of sky on the very same day for a longer while. That longer observation confirmed a rhythm of roughly an hour, and the team realised they had stumbled onto a long-period transient, or LPT.The long-period transient is a newly recognized class of radio source of unidentified objects that emit long, bright pulses of radio waves with regular, lengthy pauses between each emission. They have become apparent in the last few years.However, years earlier, in 2002, Hyman had caught a similar blast of radio flares from near the galactic centre. He then spent years waiting for a repeat which only came recently.What the telescopes sawThe paper, accepted by The Astrophysical Journal, gives the details. The source flashed bright, highly polarised radio pulses every 62.2 minutes during a 15-hour window in May 2022. Before and after that, across roughly five years of data, there was nothing.Each cycle contained two pulses: a wide main pulse and a narrow interpulse, and they didn't look alike. The main pulse was only partly polarised. The interpulse was almost 100% circularly polarised, and the two twisted in opposite directions. To the researchers, that points to emission from near both magnetic poles, with the object's spin axis tipped nearly perpendicular to its magnetic axis. They call it a near-orthogonal rotator.The twist in the plotHyman told ScienceAlert that a clean 180-degree split would be easy to explain. However, the gap between them is 165.4 degrees, about 14.6 degrees short, hinting at a more complicated magnetic structure.If the geometry were simple, the two pulses would sit exactly 180 degrees apart. They don't. That small discrepancy matters. It is because the signals probably aren't coming from the magnetic field of an ordinary pulsar. They more likely originate in a broader, messier magnetosphere. The authors say the data favour a coherent emission process called the electron cyclotron maser instability. However, they are still unable to pin down exactly what the object is or how it works.So what is it?Scientists are exploring three possibilities of LPTs being pulsars, magnetars and white dwarfs. The inconclusiveness remains because while some LPTs fulfil conditions of one of the three, others do not. Neutron stars spinning this slowly shouldn't easily produce radio emission, and white dwarfs don't explain everything either. Scientists are also exploring the possibility of whether "all LPTs" are one kind of object at all.If J1555−5631 is typical, though, this messy-magnetosphere picture might help explain some long-standing LPT irregularities, such as why their beam widths seem disconnected from their spin periods and why their polarisation angles are so often flat.The vanishing actLPT J1555−5631 hasn't been seen again. Some LPTs have returned to activity, including the one Hyman first spotted, but most haven't. Why they switch on and off remains a genuine puzzle, and the answer may lie in how their magnetospheres change over time.For now, astronomers are playing the long game. Hyman hopes a bigger catalogue will reveal patterns that allow targeted searches, though he's equally fond of serendipity and blind trawling through old data.Your child uses AI every day. articles.summary: Forgetting is as much a part of recalling memories, stories and emotions as remembering itself.
articles.body: Forgetting is as much a part of recalling memories, stories and emotions as remembering itself. But while we sometimes forget our keys, a name or even an important date, this forgetfulness can occasionally indicate something far more serious and urgent. When it comes to diseases as debilitating as Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia, scientists have long been curious to understand what actually happens in the brain.Now, researchers at Johns Hopkins University, in a study published in the journal NeuroImage: Reports in September 2026, have identified changes in two brain regions that could offer an important clue, with their findings suggesting that these areas may begin to shrink years before a person experiences noticeable memory loss.According to a ScienceDaily report dated November 14, 2026, the researchers found that while the hippocampus is an important part of the brain examined for signs of Alzheimer's, two other regions associated with memory and emotional processing could help scientists understand the development of the disease before the actual loss of memory becomes apparent.The changes could become detectable as much as five to ten years before the clinical symptoms of the disease emerge, potentially opening a new pathway for understanding its silent progression and exploring treatments during this period.Two significant regions of the brain apart from the hippocampusBut before understanding this discovery, it is important to know what these different regions of the brain are responsible for. The hippocampus is particularly important when it comes to forming and consolidating memories, which is why damage to this area is often associated with the memory difficulties experienced by people with Alzheimer's disease. But it is not the only part of the brain involved in these processes.Located near the hippocampus, the entorhinal cortex acts as an important part of the brain's memory network, helping process and retrieve previously stored information. The amygdala, meanwhile, plays a major role in processing emotions and remembering experiences that carry an emotional association. Together, these regions contribute to the way people process, retain and recall information from their lives.This research also suggests that changes in these two areas may become apparent before the hippocampus shows comparable signs of deterioration. By examining the entorhinal cortex and amygdala alongside it, scientists may be able to identify signs of the disease that could otherwise go unnoticed during its earliest stages.What the brain scans revealedFor the purpose of the scientific study, the researchers examined MRI and PET brain scans from two independent research cohorts: the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and the Biomarkers of Cognitive Decline Among Normal Individuals (BIOCARD) study. These projects included people at different stages of Alzheimer's disease, including those who had no noticeable cognitive symptoms and individuals experiencing cognitive impairment.By examining changes in the brain over time, the team found a consistent pattern across both groups. The entorhinal cortex and amygdala experienced greater relative tissue loss during the earlier stages of Alzheimer's than the hippocampus.Abnormal tau protein buildup has also been found to play a significant role in the development of Alzheimer's disease. Under normal circumstances, tau helps ensure that the internal structure of nerve cells remains stable. However, in people with Alzheimer's, this protein can accumulate abnormally and form tangled structures inside brain cells, interfering with their functioning.Using PET imaging and digital pathology, the team found that areas showing signs of tissue loss also corresponded with regions displaying tau-related changes.Could this help identify Alzheimer's earlier?One of the more promising aspects of the research is what it could mean for identifying the disease before its effects on everyday life become apparent. Alzheimer's can develop over a long period, with biological changes taking place in the brain well before a person begins experiencing significant difficulties with memory, thinking or other cognitive abilities. By the time these symptoms become noticeable, considerable changes may already have occurred.Michael Miller, a biomedical engineer at Johns Hopkins University and the study's senior author, explained that these changes could provide a window of five to ten years during which the brain is already showing signs of deterioration, even though clinical symptoms have not yet appeared. The possibility of recognising these changes earlier could eventually allow doctors to explore interventions before more extensive damage takes place.While the findings are a significant development in medical research, they should not be mistaken for a diagnostic breakthrough that is already ready for use in hospitals. Although the researchers have identified promising imaging markers, the team hopes to investigate the molecular changes taking place in these brain regions, especially those related to abnormal tau accumulation.With this study, a new pathway for further research into potential treatments has opened up, offering scientists more time to understand the processes responsible for significant tissue loss and potentially creating new avenues for treatment, especially for individuals with a family history of the disease.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 hits record one light-day distance, 50 years after launch
articles.summary: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth, marking a historic milestone nearly 50 years after its 1977 launch.
articles.body:
NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, the most distant human-made object, has reached a distance of one light-day from Earth nearly 50 years after it was launched.

The spacecraft hit the milestone on Wednesday and is now about 26 billion km away, according to NASA.

A light-day is the distance light can travel in 24 hours, which means messages sent from Earth take a day to reach Voyager 1, and another day for teams on the ground to receive a reply.

The feat is “the best illustration of just how vast space is”, said NASA scientist Tiffany Kataria. “So much of what we dream about is travelling to other stellar systems,” she told the AFP news agency. “And it took Voyager 1 nearly 50 years to get to just the edge of our own solar system, let alone to only a light-day.”

Many exoplanetary systems, she noted, are at least several light-years away. NASA expects Voyager 1 to take about 18,000 years to travel a full light-year.

Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 and its twin Voyager 2 are the only spacecraft to have reached interstellar space, the region beyond the Sun’s heliosphere. Voyager 2 is expected to reach one light-day in 2035.

Some of Voyager 1’s equipment, including its cameras, has been switched off remotely to save power, but the probe continues to study invisible phenomena such as magnetic fields.

The data helps researchers study “the gas, the dust and other material that exists between stars”, Kataria said.

Both craft carry “Golden Records”, 30cm gold-plated copper discs intended to convey the story of our world to extraterrestrials.

Earlier in their journeys, the Voyagers explored the giant planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Images of Jupiter taken by Voyager 1 first revealed the existence of rings around the planet and helped scientists understand the “really extreme vortices and weather” in its atmosphere, Kataria added.
